blood-relation.p: Pointing to a man, Rita says, "He is the son of my mother's only brother." How is the man related to Rita?
blood-relation.e: Mother's brother is Rita's maternal uncle; his son is her cousin.

blood-relation.p: A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. How is A related to D?
blood-relation.e: A and B are C's children; D is C's father, so A is D's granddaughter.

blood-relation.p: Introducing a woman, a man says, "Her mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is the woman related to the man?
blood-relation.e: The only daughter of my mother is my sister. Her daughter is my niece.

blood-relation.p: P is the brother of Q. Q is the sister of R. R is the father of S. How is P related to S?
blood-relation.e: P, Q and R are siblings. R is S's father, so P is S's uncle.

blood-relation.p: A is the mother of B. B is the sister of C. C is the father of D. How is A related to D?
blood-relation.e: A is the mother of C (B and C are siblings). D is C's child, so A is D's grandmother.

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a photograph, Vikas says, "She is the daughter of my grandfather's only son." How is she related to Vikas?
blood-relation.e: Grandfather's only son is Vikas's father. His daughter is Vikas's sister.

blood-relation.p: If A + B means A is the father of B, A − B means A is the sister of B, and A × B means A is the wife of B, which expression means P is the paternal aunt of Q?
blood-relation.e: P − R: P is R's sister. R + Q: R is Q's father. So P is Q's father's sister, the paternal aunt.

blood-relation.p: Anil's father is Sunil's son. How is Sunil related to Anil?
blood-relation.e: Sunil's son is Anil's father, so Sunil is Anil's father's father: grandfather.

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a boy, Neha says, "He is the son of my father's only daughter." How is the boy related to Neha?
blood-relation.e: Neha is her father's only daughter, so the boy is Neha's son.

blood-relation.p: M is the sister of N. N is the father of P. How is M related to P?
blood-relation.e: M is the sister of P's father, making her P's paternal aunt.

blood-relation.p: A woman says, "The man standing there is my husband's father's only son." Who is the man to the woman?
blood-relation.e: Her husband's father's only son is her husband.

blood-relation.p: X is the mother of Y. Y is the brother of Z. Z is the mother of W. How is X related to W?
blood-relation.e: X is the mother of Z, and Z is W's mother. Therefore X is W's grandmother.

blood-relation.p: A is the son of B. B is the daughter of C. How is C related to A?
blood-relation.e: B is A's parent and C is B's parent, so C is A's grandparent.

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a photograph, Arun says, "The woman is the wife of my mother's only son." If Arun is male and his mother has only one son, who is the woman?
blood-relation.e: Arun is his mother's only son, so the woman is Arun's wife.

blood-relation.p: P is Q's father. R is P's mother. S is R's husband. How is S related to Q?
blood-relation.e: R is P's mother and S is R's husband, so S is P's father. P is Q's father, so S is Q's grandfather.

blood-relation.p: Rohan says, “The woman in the photograph is my mother’s mother.” Who is the woman to Rohan?
blood-relation.e: The mother of one’s mother is the maternal grandmother.

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a girl, Sunil says, "She is the daughter of my wife's only brother." How is the girl related to Sunil?
blood-relation.e: His wife's brother is Sunil's brother-in-law; that man's daughter is Sunil's niece (by marriage).

blood-relation.p: Ramesh's mother is the sister of Kavita's father. How is Kavita related to Ramesh?
blood-relation.e: Kavita's father is Ramesh's maternal uncle, so Kavita is Ramesh's cousin.

blood-relation.p: A man says, "This boy is my father's grandson, and I have no brothers or sisters." How is the boy related to the man?
blood-relation.e: With no siblings, the only way the boy can be his father's grandson is as the man's own son.

blood-relation.p: Sita is the wife of Ram. Ram's father is Dasharath. How is Sita related to Dasharath?
blood-relation.e: Sita is married to Dasharath's son, so she is his daughter-in-law.

blood-relation.p: Mohan is the only son of Rakesh. Priti is Rakesh's daughter. How is Priti related to Mohan?
blood-relation.e: Both are Rakesh's children, and Priti is female, so she is Mohan's sister.

blood-relation.p: Vijay is the husband of Arjun's father's sister. How is Vijay related to Arjun?
blood-relation.e: Arjun's father's sister is his paternal aunt; her husband is Arjun's uncle.

blood-relation.p: A woman introduces a man as the son of her mother's brother. How is the man related to the woman?
blood-relation.e: Her mother's brother is her maternal uncle, and his son is her cousin.

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a man, Rajesh says, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is Rajesh related to the man?
blood-relation.e: The only daughter of Rajesh's mother is Rajesh's sister. She is the man's mother, so Rajesh is his maternal uncle.

blood-relation.p: A is the brother of B. C is the father of A. D is the brother of E. E is the daughter of B. Who is the uncle of D?
blood-relation.e: E is B's daughter and D is E's brother, so D is B's child. A is B's brother, so A is D's uncle.

blood-relation.p: If P $ Q means P is the brother of Q, P # Q means P is the mother of Q, and P * Q means P is the daughter of Q, which expression means M is the maternal uncle of N?
blood-relation.e: M $ K: M is K's brother. K # N: K is N's mother. So M is the brother of N's mother, the maternal uncle.

blood-relation.p: Deepak tells Nitin, "That boy is the younger of the two brothers of the daughter of my father's wife." How is the boy related to Deepak?
blood-relation.e: His father's wife is his mother; her daughter is Deepak's sister, and her brothers are Deepak and the boy. So the boy is Deepak's brother.

blood-relation.p: Introducing Reena, Sanjay says, "Her father is the only son of my father." How is Reena related to Sanjay?
blood-relation.e: Sanjay is male, so the only son of his father is Sanjay himself. Reena is therefore Sanjay's daughter.

blood-relation.p: A family has a man, his wife, their three sons, the sons' wives, and two children of each son. How many members are in the family?
blood-relation.e: 1 + 1 + 3 sons + 3 wives + 6 grandchildren = 14.

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a photograph, Lata says, "He is the son of the only son of my paternal grandfather." How is the man related to Lata?
blood-relation.e: The only son of her paternal grandfather is her father, so his son is Lata's brother.

blood-relation.p: A's mother is the sister of B, and B has a daughter C. How is A related to C?
blood-relation.e: B is A's mother's sibling, so B's daughter C is A's cousin.

blood-relation.p: P is the father of Q. Q is the son of R, a woman. S is the brother of P, and T is the daughter of S. How is R related to T?
blood-relation.e: R is Q's mother, so she is P's wife. T's father S is P's brother, so R is T's aunt.

blood-relation.p: M is the son of N. N and O are sisters. P is the mother of O. How is P related to M?
blood-relation.e: N and O are sisters, so P is also N's mother. N is M's mother, so P is M's grandmother.

blood-relation.p: Kamal is the son of Anil. Anil's sister Bina has a son, Chetan, whose wife is Ekta. How is Ekta related to Kamal?
blood-relation.e: Chetan is the son of Kamal's paternal aunt, so he is Kamal's cousin. Ekta is Chetan's wife.

blood-relation.p: If A + B means A is the son of B, A − B means A is the wife of B, and A × B means A is the brother of B, which expression means P is the daughter-in-law of Q?
blood-relation.e: P − R: P is R's wife. R + Q: R is Q's son. So P is the wife of Q's son, Q's daughter-in-law.

blood-relation.p: Neel has no brothers and one sister. He says, "Sonia's father is my father's only son-in-law." How is Sonia related to Neel?
blood-relation.e: His father's only son-in-law is Neel's sister's husband. Sonia is that man's daughter, so she is Neel's niece.

blood-relation.p: Raj and Mili are the son and daughter of Mr. Verma. Raj's wife is Tina, and Mili's son is Bunty. How is Tina related to Bunty?
blood-relation.e: Raj is Bunty's maternal uncle, so Raj's wife Tina is Bunty's aunt.

blood-relation.p: X and Y are brothers. R is the father of Y. S is the brother of T, and T is the mother of R. How is S related to X?
blood-relation.e: R is X's father too. T is R's mother, so T is X's grandmother, and S, T's brother, is X's grandmother's brother (great-uncle).

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a lady, a man says, "The son of her only brother is the brother of my wife." How is the lady related to the man?
blood-relation.e: Her brother's son is the man's wife's brother, so her brother is the man's father-in-law. The lady is his father-in-law's sister.

blood-relation.p: A + B means A is the mother of B; A − B means A is the brother of B; A × B means A is the husband of B; A ÷ B means A is the daughter of B. If P × Q + R − S, how is P related to S?
blood-relation.e: P is Q's husband, Q is R's mother, and R is S's brother. So Q is S's mother and P, her husband, is S's father.

blood-relation.p: A + B means A is the mother of B; A − B means A is the brother of B; A × B means A is the husband of B; A ÷ B means A is the daughter of B. If L ÷ M × N + O, how is L related to O?
blood-relation.e: M is N's husband and N is O's mother, so M is O's father. L is M's daughter, so L is O's sister.

blood-relation.p: Sunita is the wife of the only son of Rani's paternal grandmother. How is Sunita related to Rani?
blood-relation.e: The only son of Rani's paternal grandmother is Rani's father, and his wife is Rani's mother.

blood-relation.p: Q's mother is the sister of P and the daughter of M. S is the daughter of P and the sister of T. How is M related to T?
blood-relation.e: Q's mother is M's daughter and P's sister, so P is also M's child. T is P's child, so M is T's grandparent.

blood-relation.p: A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. E is D's mother. How is A related to E?
blood-relation.e: A is C's daughter, C is D's child and D is E's son. So A is three generations below E: her great-granddaughter.

blood-relation.p: Looking at a portrait, a man says, "I have no brother or sister, but that man's father is my father's son." Whose portrait is it?
blood-relation.e: With no siblings, 'my father's son' is the speaker himself. The man in the portrait is the speaker's son.

blood-relation.p: Pointing to a man, a woman says, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is the woman related to the man?
blood-relation.e: The only daughter of the woman's mother is the woman herself, so she is the man's mother.

blood-relation.p: A is the brother of B. B is the son of C. D is the father of C. E is the daughter of D. Which statement is definitely true?
blood-relation.e: C and E are both D's children, so E is C's sister. C is A's parent, so E is A's aunt; D is A's grandfather.

blood-relation.p: P + Q means P is the father of Q; P − Q means P is the wife of Q; P × Q means P is the brother of Q. What does A − B + C × D mean?
blood-relation.e: A is B's wife, B is C's father and C is D's brother. So B is D's father too, and A is D's mother.

blood-relation.p: Tanu is the only daughter of Sapna's husband's brother. Rima is the wife of Tanu's father. How is Rima related to Sapna?
blood-relation.e: Tanu's father is the brother of Sapna's husband, and Rima is his wife, so Rima is Sapna's sister-in-law.

blood-relation.p: Gopal is the father of Hari. Hari's sister Indu is married to Jatin, whose mother is Kalpana. How is Kalpana related to Gopal?
blood-relation.e: Indu is Gopal's daughter, and Kalpana is the mother of Indu's husband, so she is his daughter's mother-in-law.

puzzles.p: Five friends A, B, C, D and E have different heights. A is taller than B but shorter than C. D is taller than C. E is shorter than B. Who is the tallest?
puzzles.e: Chain: D > C > A > B > E. D is the tallest.

puzzles.p: Five friends A, B, C, D and E have different heights. A is taller than B but shorter than C. D is taller than C. E is shorter than B. Who is the second shortest?
puzzles.e: D > C > A > B > E. B is second from the bottom.

puzzles.p: Five people P, Q, R, S, T live on five floors (1 is the lowest). P lives above Q but below R. T lives on floor 1. S lives immediately below P. Who lives on floor 3?
puzzles.e: T = 1. S sits directly under P and Q is below P too, so Q = 2, S = 3, P = 4, R = 5.

puzzles.p: Three boxes are labelled Apples, Oranges and Mixed, and every label is wrong. You take one fruit from the box labelled Mixed and it is an apple. What does the box labelled Oranges contain?
puzzles.e: The 'Mixed' box must be pure, so it is apples. The 'Oranges' box cannot be oranges, and apples are taken, so it is mixed.

puzzles.p: A is twice as old as B. B is 3 years older than C. C is 12 years old. How old is A?
Four people P, Q, R and S sit in a row, from left to right. P is not at either end. Q is immediately to the right of S. R is at the left end. Who is at the right end?
puzzles.e: R is first. P must be 2nd or 3rd; S and Q must be adjacent, which only works if P is 2nd, S 3rd and Q 4th.

puzzles.p: A finished ahead of B. C finished behind D. B finished ahead of D. Who finished last?
puzzles.e: A, B, D, C is the only consistent order, so C is last.

puzzles.p: Rahul ranks 12th from the top and 29th from the bottom in a class. How many students are in the class?
Four tasks A, B, C and D must be completed. A is before B, C is after B, and D is before A. Which task must be first?
puzzles.e: The constraints imply D < A < B < C, so D must be first.

puzzles.p: A clock loses 5 minutes every hour. If it is correct at noon, what time will it show after 6 real hours?
puzzles.e: It loses 30 minutes in 6 hours, so at real 6 PM it shows 5:30 PM.

puzzles.p: Three switches outside a closed room control one bulb inside. You may enter the room only once. How can you identify the correct switch?
puzzles.c: Use bulb warmth and whether it is lit
w: It is impossible in all cases
puzzles.e: Turn one switch on for a few minutes, turn it off, turn another on, then enter. Lit means the second; warm but off means the first; cool and off means the third.

puzzles.p: A bag contains 4 red and 5 blue balls. What is the minimum number of balls you must draw without looking to guarantee two of the same colour?
puzzles.e: With two colours, the first two could differ; the third must match one of them.

puzzles.p: A father is 4 times as old as his son. In 20 years, he will be twice as old as his son. How old is the son now?
puzzles.e: Let son's age be x; father is 4x. Then 4x+20 = 2(x+20), so x=10.

puzzles.p: A number is doubled and then 9 is added, giving 31. What is the number?
A, B and C finish a race. A finishes before B. C finishes after B. Who finishes second?
puzzles.e: The order is A, B, C.

puzzles.p: Five people each shake hands with every other person exactly once. How many handshakes occur?
puzzles.e: The number is 5×4÷2 = 10.

puzzles.p: If all bloops are razzies and all razzies are lazzies, which statement must be true?
puzzles.e: The first group is entirely contained in the second, which is contained in the third.

puzzles.p: In a row of children, Anu is 7th from the left and 10th from the right. How many children are in the row?
If today is Wednesday, what day will it be 10 days from now?
puzzles.e: 10 days = 1 week + 3 days, and 3 days after Wednesday is Saturday.

puzzles.p: P is taller than Q, and Q is taller than R. Who is the shortest?
puzzles.e: P > Q > R, so R is the shortest.

puzzles.p: A man walks 5 km north, then turns right and walks 3 km. Which direction is he facing now?
puzzles.e: Turning right while facing north makes him face east.

puzzles.p: Ravi is 15th from the front in a queue of 40 people. What is his position from the back?
puzzles.e: Position from the back = 40 − 15 + 1 = 26.

puzzles.p: In a certain code, CAT is written as DBU. How is BAT written in that code?
puzzles.e: Each letter moves one place forward: B→C, A→B, T→U.

puzzles.p: Find the odd one out: Apple, Mango, Potato, Banana.
puzzles.e: Potato is a vegetable (a tuber); the others are fruits.

puzzles.p: What comes next in the series 2, 4, 8, 16, ?
puzzles.e: Each term is double the previous one: 16 × 2 = 32.

puzzles.p: A clock shows exactly 3:00. What is the angle between the hour and minute hands?
puzzles.e: The hands are 3 hour-marks apart, and each mark is 30°, so 3 × 30° = 90°.

puzzles.p: If the day before yesterday was Thursday, what day is tomorrow?
puzzles.e: Yesterday was Friday and today is Saturday, so tomorrow is Sunday.

puzzles.p: Five books are stacked. Green is on top, Blue at the bottom, Red just above Blue, and Yellow just below Green. The fifth book is White. Which book is in the middle?
puzzles.e: From the top: Green, Yellow, ?, Red, Blue. The only free place, the middle, is White.

puzzles.p: If NORTH is coded as OPSUI, how is SOUTH coded?
puzzles.e: Each letter moves one place forward: S→T, O→P, U→V, T→U, H→I.

puzzles.p: In a class, Meena ranks 9th from the top. Rita is 5 ranks below Meena and 20th from the bottom. How many students are in the class?
puzzles.e: Rita is 14th from the top and 20th from the bottom, so the total is 14 + 20 − 1 = 33.

puzzles.p: If 1 January 2023 was a Sunday, what day of the week was 1 January 2024?
puzzles.e: 2023 is not a leap year: 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 day, so the day moves one forward to Monday.

puzzles.p: A man walks 10 m south, turns left and walks 6 m, then turns left again and walks 10 m. Where is he relative to his starting point?
puzzles.e: Facing south, a left turn means east (6 m); facing east, another left means north (10 m), cancelling the 10 m south. He is 6 m east.

puzzles.p: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 4:20?
puzzles.e: Hour hand: 4 × 30 + 20 × 0.5 = 130°. Minute hand: 20 × 6 = 120°. Difference = 10°.

puzzles.p: Find the next term: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ?
puzzles.e: The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, so the next difference is 11: 27 + 11 = 38.

puzzles.p: In a tournament, each of 8 teams plays every other team exactly once. How many matches are played?
puzzles.e: Number of pairs = 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28.

puzzles.p: A cube painted red on all faces is cut into 27 equal smaller cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
puzzles.e: Two-face cubes sit on the edges, excluding corners: 12 edges × (3 − 2) = 12.

puzzles.p: Five people A–E have different weights. A is heavier than B and C. D is lighter than C. E is heavier than A. Who is the second heaviest?
puzzles.e: E > A, and A is heavier than B and C, while D is lighter than C. So E is heaviest and A second.

puzzles.p: If 15 March 2021 was a Monday, what day of the week was 15 March 2022?
puzzles.e: The year in between contains February 2022, which has 28 days, so it is 365 days: one odd day. Monday + 1 = Tuesday.

puzzles.p: Find the next term: 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, ?
puzzles.e: The differences double: 1, 2, 4, 8, so the next is 16: 17 + 16 = 33.

puzzles.p: In a code, 'sky is blue' is 'ta pa ka', 'blue is good' is 'ka ma ta' and 'good day' is 'ma ri'. What is the code for 'sky'?
puzzles.e: 'is blue' is common to the first two, matching 'ta ka'. So 'sky' is the remaining word, 'pa'.

puzzles.p: The sum of the present ages of a father and son is 50. Five years ago the father was 7 times as old as the son. What is the son's present age?
puzzles.e: F + S = 50 and F − 5 = 7(S − 5). Substituting F = 50 − S gives 45 − S = 7S − 35, so S = 10.

puzzles.p: A cube painted on all faces is cut into 64 equal smaller cubes. How many small cubes have no painted face?
puzzles.e: Each edge has 4 small cubes; the unpainted core is (4 − 2)³ = 8.

puzzles.p: A says, "B is lying." B says, "C is lying." C says, "A and B are both lying." Who is telling the truth?
puzzles.e: If C were truthful, A would be lying, so B would be truthful: a contradiction. So C lies, B's claim is true, and A's claim is false.

puzzles.p: At what time between 3 and 4 o'clock are the hands of a clock together?
puzzles.e: The minute hand gains 11/2° per minute and must make up 90°: 90 ÷ 5.5 = 180/11 = 16 4/11 minutes.

puzzles.p: Starting from point P, Ram walks 20 m west, turns right and walks 15 m, then turns right again and walks 40 m. How far is he from P?
puzzles.e: He ends 20 m east and 15 m north of P. Distance = √(20² + 15²) = √625 = 25 m.

puzzles.p: On what day of the week did 15 August 1947 fall?
puzzles.e: Counting odd days: 1600 years → 0, 300 years → 1, 46 years (11 leap) → 57 ≡ 1, Jan–Jul 1947 → 2, plus 15 days → 1. Total 5 odd days: Friday.

puzzles.p: A clock is set right at 8 a.m. It gains 10 minutes every 24 hours. What is the true time when it shows 1 p.m. the next day?
puzzles.e: The clock shows 29 hours elapsed. It shows 24 h 10 min per 24 true hours, so true time = 29 × 24 ÷ (145/6) = 28.8 h = 28 h 48 min after 8 a.m.

puzzles.p: Three boxes; one holds gold. Box 1: 'The gold is here.' Box 2: 'The gold is not here.' Box 3: 'The gold is not in Box 1.' Exactly one statement is true. Where is the gold?
puzzles.e: Gold in Box 1 makes statements 1 and 2 true; in Box 3, statements 2 and 3 are true. Only Box 2 leaves exactly one true statement (Box 3's).

puzzles.p: A frog at the bottom of a 20 m well climbs 5 m each day and slips back 4 m each night. On which day does it reach the top?
puzzles.e: After 15 days and nights it is at 15 m. On day 16 it climbs 5 m to reach 20 m before slipping.

puzzles.p: Which number replaces the question mark: 4, 9, 25, 49, ?, 169
puzzles.e: These are squares of consecutive primes: 2², 3², 5², 7², 11², 13².

dices.p: A standard die shows 1 on top, 2 at the front and 3 on the right. What number is on the bottom face?
dices.e: The bottom is opposite the top: 7 − 1 = 6.

dices.p: A standard die has 1 on top and 2 at the front. Which number is at the back?
dices.e: The back is opposite the front: 7 − 2 = 5.

dices.p: On a standard die the top shows 5. What is the sum of the numbers on the four side faces?
dices.e: All faces sum to 21. Top 5 and bottom 2 make 7, so the sides total 21 − 7 = 14.

dices.p: A standard die has 6 on top and 3 at the front. Which number is at the back?
dices.e: The back is opposite the front: 7 − 3 = 4.

dices.p: A standard die is thrown twice and shows 3 then 5 on top. What is the total of the two bottom faces?
dices.e: Bottoms are 7 − 3 = 4 and 7 − 5 = 2. Total = 6.

dices.p: On a standard die, which number is opposite 4?
dices.e: On a standard die, opposite faces sum to 7; 7 − 4 = 3.

dices.p: A standard die shows 2 on top. What number is on the bottom?
dices.e: Opposite faces on a standard die sum to 7; 7 − 2 = 5.

dices.p: A standard die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an even number?
dices.e: Even faces are 2, 4 and 6: 3 favourable outcomes out of 6.

dices.p: Two standard dice are rolled. What is the maximum possible sum?
dices.e: Each die can show at most 6, so the maximum is 6 + 6 = 12.

dices.p: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the minimum possible sum?
dices.e: The lowest face on each die is 1, so 1 + 1 = 2.

dices.p: On a standard die, the face opposite 5 is what number?
dices.e: Opposite faces on a standard die sum to 7.

dices.p: A cube net is a cross: 1 in the centre, 2 above it, 3 below it, 4 on its left, 5 on its right, and 6 attached below 3. Which number is opposite 1?
dices.e: In the vertical strip 2-1-3-6, faces one apart are opposite: 2 opposite 3 and 1 opposite 6.

dices.p: A cube net has four squares in a column, A, B, C, D from top to bottom, with E attached to the left of B and F to the right of B. Which letter is opposite A?
dices.e: In a column of four, alternate squares are opposite: A–C and B–D. The two side flaps E and F are opposite each other.

dices.p: Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability that both show the same number?
dices.e: There are 6 doubles out of 36 outcomes: 6/36 = 1/6.

dices.p: A standard die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
dices.e: Only 5 and 6 qualify: 2 out of 6 = 1/3.

dices.p: What is the sum of the numbers on all six faces of a standard die?
dices.e: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21 (three opposite pairs of 7).

dices.p: Three standard dice show 2, 4 and 5 on top. What is the sum of their bottom faces?
dices.e: Bottoms are 7 − 2 = 5, 7 − 4 = 3 and 7 − 5 = 2, totalling 10.

dices.p: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube (die) have?
dices.e: A cube has 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 corners (vertices).

dices.p: Two standard dice are rolled. In how many of the 36 outcomes is the sum 7?
A standard die rests with 3 on top. Which of these numbers cannot be on any of its four side faces?
dices.e: 4 is opposite 3, so it is on the bottom, not on a side.

dices.p: A die (faces 1–6, not necessarily standard) is seen in two positions. Position 1: 1 on top, 2 in front, 3 on the right. Position 2: 1 on top, 3 in front, 5 on the right. Which number is opposite 2?
dices.e: 1 stays on top, so the die only turned about the vertical axis: 3 moved from right to front, so the old back face is now on the right. The back was opposite the front (2), so 5 is opposite 2.

dices.p: A die is seen in two positions. Position 1: 4 on top, 1 in front, 2 on the right. Position 2: 4 on top, 2 in front, 6 on the right. Which number is opposite 1?
dices.e: With 4 fixed on top, the right face (2) has turned to the front, so the old back face now shows on the right. The back was opposite the front (1), so 6 is opposite 1.

dices.p: A die is seen in two positions. Position 1: 5 on top, 3 in front, 6 on the right. Position 2: 5 on top, 6 in front, 2 on the right. Which number is opposite 3?
dices.e: 5 stays on top, so the die spun about the vertical axis: 6 moved from right to front and the old back (opposite 3) came to the right. So 2 is opposite 3.

dices.p: Three standard dice are stacked in a column on a table, and the top face of the stack shows 5. What is the total number of dots on the hidden faces (faces touching each other or the table)?
dices.e: Top die: hidden bottom = 2. Middle and bottom dice each hide a top and bottom pair = 7 + 7. Total 2 + 14 = 16.

dices.p: Four standard dice are stacked in a column, and the top face shows 6. What is the total of all the hidden horizontal faces?
dices.e: The top die hides 1 (opposite 6). Each of the other three dice hides a top–bottom pair worth 7: 1 + 21 = 22.

dices.p: A standard die shows 1 on top and 2 in front. It is tipped over its far edge (away from the viewer) once. Which number is now on top?
dices.e: Tipping away moves the front face up to the top and the top face to the back, so 2 comes on top.

dices.p: A die shows 1 on top and 2 in front. It is rolled once to the right (onto its right face). Which number now faces the front?
dices.e: A roll to the right turns the die about the front–back axis, so the front face stays at the front.

dices.p: Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 10?
Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
A cube net is a row of four squares 1, 2, 3, 4 from left to right, with 5 attached above square 1 and 6 attached below square 4. Which number is opposite 5?
dices.e: The row of four wraps around to form the side faces; the squares attached on opposite sides of the row become top and bottom, so 5 and 6 are opposite.

dices.p: A cube net is a cross: P in the centre, Q above, R below, S on the left, T on the right, and U attached below R. Which letter is opposite S?
dices.e: The two arms on either side of the centre square fold to opposite faces, so S is opposite T.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in two positions. Position 1: 2 on top, 5 in front, 4 on the right. Position 2: 1 on top, 2 in front, 3 on the right. Which number is opposite 2?
dices.e: 2 appears next to 5, 4, 1, 3, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 2, 6, must be opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in two positions. Position 1: 3 on top, 4 in front, 6 on the right. Position 2: 1 on top, 2 in front, 3 on the right. Which number is opposite 3?
dices.e: 3 appears next to 4, 6, 1, 2, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 3, 5, must be opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in two positions. Position 1: 2 on top, 1 in front, 6 on the right. Position 2: 6 on top, 5 in front, 3 on the right. Which number is opposite 6?
dices.e: 6 appears next to 2, 1, 5, 3, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 6, 4, must be opposite.

dices.p: Two views of the same die are given. Position 1: 5 on top, 1 in front, 6 on the right. Position 2: 3 on top, 4 in front, 5 on the right. Which number is opposite 5?
dices.e: 5 appears next to 1, 6, 3, 4, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 5, 2, must be opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in two positions. Position 1: 1 on top, 2 in front, 3 on the right. Position 2: 4 on top, 3 in front, 2 on the right. Which number is opposite 1?
dices.e: 2 and 3 are seen together, so they are adjacent. Both 1 and 4 touch 2 and 3, and the only two faces touching a pair of adjacent faces are opposite each other. So 4 is opposite 1.

dices.p: Two views of one die are described. Position 1: 4 on top, 3 in front, 2 on the right. Position 2: 3 on top, 4 in front, 6 on the right. Which number is opposite 2?
dices.e: 3 and 4 are adjacent. Both 2 and 6 touch 3 and 4, and the only two faces touching a pair of adjacent faces are opposite each other. So 6 is opposite 2.

dices.p: A standard die shows 1 on top and 2 in front. It is tipped over its far edge (away from the viewer) twice. Which number is now on top?
dices.e: Each tip brings the front face to the top. After two quarter-turns the original top has gone to the bottom, so its opposite, 6, is on top.

dices.p: Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability that at least one shows a 6?
dices.e: P(no six) = (5/6)² = 25/36, so P(at least one six) = 11/36.

dices.p: Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the numbers is even?
dices.e: The product is odd only when both are odd: (1/2)² = 1/4. So P(even) = 3/4.

dices.p: Two standard dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is a prime number?

A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in three positions. Position 1: 2 on top, 1 in front, 6 on the right. Position 2: 6 on top, 5 in front, 3 on the right. Position 3: 5 on top, 6 in front, 1 on the right. Which number is opposite 1?
dices.e: 1 is seen with 2, 5 and 6, so they are adjacent to it. 6 is seen with 2, 1, 5 and 3, so 4 is opposite 6. That leaves 3 opposite 1.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in three positions. Position 1: 1 on top, 2 in front, 3 on the right. Position 2: 4 on top, 3 in front, 2 on the right. Position 3: 3 on top, 4 in front, 6 on the right. Which number is opposite 5?
dices.e: 3 is seen with 1, 2, 4 and 6, so all of them are adjacent to 3. The only face never seen with 3 is 5, so 5 and 3 are opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in three positions. Position 1: 3 on top, 4 in front, 5 on the right. Position 2: 1 on top, 4 in front, 2 on the right. Position 3: 1 on top, 5 in front, 4 on the right. Which number is opposite 2?
dices.e: 4 is seen with 3, 5, 1 and 2, so 6 is opposite 4. 1 is seen with 4, 2 and 5, so 1 is opposite 3 (6 is taken). The remaining pair is 2 and 5.

dices.p: A cube has the letters A–F on its faces. It is seen in three positions. Position 1: A on top, B in front, C on the right. Position 2: A on top, D in front, B on the right. Position 3: E on top, C in front, B on the right. Which letter is opposite B?
dices.e: B appears next to A, C, D, E, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with B, F, must be opposite.

dices.p: A cube has the letters A–F on its faces. It is seen in three positions. Position 1: E on top, C in front, F on the right. Position 2: B on top, A in front, D on the right. Position 3: D on top, E in front, F on the right. Which letter is opposite D?
dices.e: D appears next to B, A, E, F, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with D, C, must be opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in three positions. Position 1: 2 on top, 5 in front, 4 on the right. Position 2: 3 on top, 6 in front, 5 on the right. Position 3: 6 on top, 3 in front, 1 on the right. Which number is opposite 5?
dices.e: 5 appears next to 2, 4, 3, 6, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 5, 1, must be opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in three positions. Position 1: 3 on top, 4 in front, 5 on the right. Position 2: 1 on top, 6 in front, 4 on the right. Position 3: 6 on top, 1 in front, 2 on the right. Which number is opposite 4?
dices.e: 4 appears next to 3, 5, 1, 6, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 4, 2, must be opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in three positions. Position 1: 2 on top, 6 in front, 5 on the right. Position 2: 1 on top, 5 in front, 3 on the right. Position 3: 4 on top, 2 in front, 1 on the right. Which number is opposite 1?
dices.e: 1 appears next to 5, 3, 4, 2, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 1, 6, must be opposite.

dices.p: A die (faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, not necessarily a standard die) is seen in three positions. Position 1: 4 on top, 3 in front, 5 on the right. Position 2: 3 on top, 4 in front, 2 on the right. Position 3: 6 on top, 2 in front, 4 on the right. Which number is opposite 4?
dices.e: 4 appears next to 3, 5, 2, 6, so all of these are adjacent to it. The only face never seen with 4, 1, must be opposite.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of x?
I. x² = 16
II. x > 0
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives x = ±4, so it is not enough alone. II alone gives nothing specific. Together x = 4.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is Ravi older than Sita?
I. Ravi is 5 years older than Meena.
II. Meena is older than Sita.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together: Ravi > Meena > Sita, so yes. Neither statement alone links Ravi to Sita.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the area of a rectangle?
I. Its perimeter is 30 cm.
II. Its length is twice its breadth.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together: l + b = 15 and l = 2b give b = 5, l = 10, area 50 cm². Each alone leaves two unknowns.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the cost price of an article?
I. It was sold at a profit of 20%.
II. The selling price was ₹600.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together CP = 600 × 100/120 = ₹500. Neither alone is enough.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is Tina's age?
I. Tina is twice as old as her brother, who is 9.
II. Tina is 5 years older than her sister.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I alone gives 18. II alone gives only a relation to an unknown age.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of y?
I. 2y + 3 = 11
II. y² − 16 = 0
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives y = 4 exactly. II gives y = ±4, which is ambiguous.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is the number n even?
I. n is a multiple of 3.
II. n is a multiple of 6.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Every multiple of 6 is even, so II is sufficient. Multiples of 3 can be odd or even.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the number?
I. It is a two-digit multiple of 11.
II. The sum of its digits is 8.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives 11, 22, …, 99; II alone gives many numbers. Together only 44 works.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of z?
I. z is a prime number.
II. z is less than 20.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together z could be 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 or 19: still not unique.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is integer n divisible by 6?
I. n is divisible by 2.
II. n is divisible by 3.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Divisibility by both 2 and 3 is sufficient for divisibility by 6; neither condition alone guarantees it.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of x?
I. x + y = 10
II. y = 4
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I alone leaves two variables. II alone gives only y. Together x = 6.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is a triangle right-angled?
I. Its sides are 3, 4 and 5.
II. Its perimeter is 12.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: The 3-4-5 side lengths establish a right triangle. A perimeter of 12 alone does not.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is x greater than 0?
I. x² = 9.
II. x is not negative.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I allows −3 or 3. II permits zero and positive values. Together x is 3, so the answer is yes.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is 5 a factor of the integer N?
I. N is even.
II. The last digit of N is 0.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: II: any integer ending in 0 is divisible by 5 (and 10). I alone allows N = 2 or N = 10.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the average of five numbers?
I. Their sum is 75.
II. The largest of them is 20.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: The question already says there are five numbers, so I gives the average directly: 75 ÷ 5 = 15. II alone gives no total.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is integer n even?
I. n is divisible by 4.
II. n is greater than 10.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Every multiple of 4 is even, so I alone answers yes. II alone allows both odd and even values.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is x?
I. x + 3 = 10
II. x is positive.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives x = 7 directly. II only restricts the sign.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the area of a rectangle?
I. Its length is 8 cm.
II. Its width is 5 cm.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Area needs both dimensions: 8 × 5 = 40 cm². Neither statement alone is enough.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is x greater than 0?
I. x² = 36
II. x is not negative.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I allows x = 6 or −6. II alone allows x = 0. Together x = 6, so the answer is yes.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is Ramesh's monthly salary?
I. His annual salary is ₹6,00,000.
II. He saves ₹10,000 a month.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives ₹6,00,000 ÷ 12 = ₹50,000 per month. Savings alone say nothing about salary.

data-sufficiency.p:
How many students are in the class?
I. Ravi is 10th from the top.
II. Ravi is 21st from the bottom.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together: 10 + 21 − 1 = 30. Each rank alone gives no total.

data-sufficiency.p:
On which day of the week is 20 March this year?
I. 20 March is a public holiday.
II. 15 March is a Friday.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: II alone: 20 March is 5 days after Friday, i.e. Wednesday. I gives no day of the week.

data-sufficiency.p:
Who is the oldest among P, Q and R?
I. P is older than Q.
II. R is older than Q.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Even together we only know Q is the youngest; P and R are never compared.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of a?
I. a + b = 12
II. a − b = 4
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Adding the equations gives 2a = 16, so a = 8. Each equation alone has two unknowns.

data-sufficiency.p:
Who is the tallest among A, B and C?
I. A is taller than B.
II. C is shorter than B.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together A > B > C, so A is tallest. I alone says nothing about C; II alone says nothing about A.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the speed of the car?
I. It is faster than the bus.
II. It covers 180 km in 3 hours at a uniform speed.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: II gives 180 ÷ 3 = 60 km/h. I is only a comparison.

data-sufficiency.p:
In which direction is the school from the house?
I. The school is 2 km north of the temple.
II. The temple is 2 km east of the house.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together the school is 2 km east and 2 km north of the house, i.e. north-east. Each statement alone does not involve both places.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the perimeter of the square?
I. Its area is 49 cm².
II. Its diagonal is longer than its side.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives side 7 cm and perimeter 28 cm. II is true of every square.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is Raj's age?
I. Raj is older than Sunil.
II. Sunil is 20 years old.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together we only know Raj is older than 20, not his exact age.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is Monday a working day for the office?
I. The office is closed on Sundays.
II. The office works six days a week.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together it closes only on Sunday, so Monday is a working day. II alone does not say which day is off.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is Mohan's rank from the top in a class of 40?
I. He is 5 ranks below Sohan.
II. His rank from the bottom is 15.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: II: 40 − 15 + 1 = 26th from the top. I depends on Sohan's unknown rank.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the cost of one pen?
I. 5 pens and 3 pencils cost ₹65.
II. 3 pens and 5 pencils cost ₹55.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Solving 5p + 3c = 65 and 3p + 5c = 55 gives p = 10. Each equation alone has two unknowns.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is x > y?
I. x = 2y
II. y > 0
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together x − y = y > 0, so yes. I alone fails for negative y (x = −4, y = −2).

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the two-digit number?
I. The sum of its digits is 9.
II. The tens digit is twice the units digit.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together t + u = 9 and t = 2u give u = 3, t = 6: the number is 63. Either alone allows several numbers.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is the integer k a multiple of 15?
I. k is a multiple of 5.
II. k is a multiple of 9.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together k is a multiple of 45, hence of 15. Alone, 5 or 9 are counter-examples.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the area of a circle?
I. Its diameter is longer than 10 cm.
II. Its circumference is 44 cm.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: II: 2πr = 44 gives r = 7 cm and area 154 cm². I gives only a range.

data-sufficiency.p:
How old is Neha?
I. Neha is 4 years younger than Pooja.
II. Pooja is twice as old as Neha.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together P = N + 4 and P = 2N give N = 4. Each alone relates two unknowns.

data-sufficiency.p:
How many sisters does Raju have?
I. Raju's mother has exactly 3 children.
II. Raju has exactly one brother.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together the three children are Raju, his brother and one more child, who must be a girl: 1 sister.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is x an integer?
I. 2x is an integer.
II. 3x is an integer.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together x = 3x − 2x is an integer. Alone, x = 1/2 satisfies I and x = 1/3 satisfies II.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is a > b?
I. a² > b²
II. a + b > 0
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) > 0 and a + b > 0 force a − b > 0. Alone, a = −3, b = 1 breaks I and a = 1, b = 2 breaks II.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the remainder when the integer n is divided by 6?
I. n leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3.
II. n is odd.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I allows n = 1 or 4 (mod 6); II removes 4, so the remainder is 1. II alone allows 1, 3 or 5.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is the product xy positive?
I. x + y > 0
II. x/y > 0
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: x/y > 0 means x and y share a sign, so xy > 0. I alone allows x = 3, y = −1.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of the prime k?
I. k lies between 20 and 30.
II. k + 2 is also prime.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I allows 23 or 29; with II, 25 is not prime but 31 is, so k = 29. II alone allows 3, 5, 11, …

data-sufficiency.p:
x, y and z are integers. Is xyz = 0?
I. yz = 6
II. xy = 0
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: II: xy = 0 already makes xyz = 0. I says y and z are non-zero but x is unknown.

data-sufficiency.p:
P is 5 km from Q. How far is P from R?
I. R is 3 km from Q.
II. Q lies on the straight segment joining P and R.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Together PR = PQ + QR = 8 km. I alone allows anything from 2 to 8 km.

data-sufficiency.p:
Is the integer N divisible by 12?
I. N is divisible by 6.
II. N is divisible by 2.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: Every multiple of 6 is already even, so II adds nothing; 12 and 18 both satisfy both statements but only 12 is divisible by 12.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of x?
I. x² − 5x + 6 = 0
II. x is a prime number.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives x = 2 or 3, and both are prime, so even together x is not unique.

data-sufficiency.p:
Among five friends, who is the heaviest?
I. A is heavier than B and C but lighter than D.
II. E is lighter than B.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives D > A > B, C but E is unplaced. II puts E below B, so D is the heaviest.

data-sufficiency.p:
What is the value of x + y?
I. 2x + 2y = 18
II. x − y = 3
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: I gives x + y = 9 directly. II alone gives only the difference.

data-sufficiency.p:
In a code language, what does 'pit' mean?
I. 'pit nok sa' means 'books are costly' and 'sa ra pit' means 'costly pens are'.
II. 'nok sa' means 'books costly'.
o: Both I and II together are sufficient
data-sufficiency.e: From I, 'pit sa' stand for 'are costly' in some order. II fixes 'sa' as 'books' or 'costly', so 'pit' must be 'are'. II alone says nothing about 'pit'.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The school has announced that students must wear ID cards from Monday.
Assumptions: I. Students have ID cards or can get them.  II. All students will follow the rule willingly.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: I must hold for the order to make sense. Nothing in the statement assumes willing compliance.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: "Use Shine toothpaste for stronger teeth." (an advertisement)
Assumptions: I. People want strong teeth.  II. Shine is the only toothpaste that strengthens teeth.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: An advert assumes its audience wants the benefit. Exclusivity is not assumed.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The manager told the team, "Submit your reports by Friday, or the project will be delayed."
Assumptions: I. The reports can be submitted by Friday.  II. The project cannot proceed without the reports.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: Both are needed for the demand and the warning to be sensible.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Sales of the product fell after its price was raised.
Conclusions: I. The price rise caused the fall in sales.  II. The company should lower the price.
assumptions-conclusions.e: The statement shows a sequence, not a cause, and gives no basis for a recommendation.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: All the rooms in the hotel are air-conditioned. Room 12 is in the hotel.
Conclusions: I. Room 12 is air-conditioned.  II. All air-conditioned rooms are in the hotel.
assumptions-conclusions.e: I follows directly. II reverses 'All', which is not valid.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Many people in the colony have fallen ill because the drinking water is contaminated.
Courses of action: I. The authorities should supply clean water immediately.  II. People should ignore the problem.
assumptions-conclusions.e: I addresses the cause. II is harmful and does not follow.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Road accidents have risen sharply in the city.
Courses of action: I. Traffic police should enforce speed limits strictly.  II. The government should ban all vehicles in the city.
assumptions-conclusions.e: I is a reasonable, proportionate step. II is extreme and impractical.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The train arrives on time only if there is no fog. Today there is dense fog.
Conclusions: I. The train will not arrive on time today.  II. The train has already left late.
assumptions-conclusions.e: 'Only if no fog' means fog rules out arriving on time, so I follows. II adds a fact not given.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The company introduced an online booking system to reduce waiting time.
Assumptions: I. Waiting time was a concern. II. Customers can access or be assisted with online booking.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The stated purpose presumes waiting time is a concern and that the system can be used by at least the intended users.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly.
Conclusions: I. Some roses fade quickly.  II. Some flowers are roses.
assumptions-conclusions.e: II follows by converting 'All roses are flowers'. The flowers that fade quickly need not include any roses, so I does not follow.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The city has advised residents to conserve water during the summer.
Assumptions: I. Water availability may be constrained. II. Residents can influence their water use.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The advice implies a reason to conserve and assumes individual usage can be changed.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: No poets are careless. Some writers are poets.
Conclusions: I. Some writers are not careless. II. All writers are poets.
assumptions-conclusions.e: The writers who are poets cannot be careless. Nothing says all writers are poets.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A school will hold extra classes for students who have not met the required standard.
Assumptions: I. Some students may need additional support. II. Extra classes can help some students improve.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The policy presumes a support need and that extra classes are a reasonable way to address it.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: All cats are animals. All animals are living beings.
Conclusions: I. All cats are living beings.  II. All living beings are cats.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Cats ⊂ animals ⊂ living beings gives I. II reverses 'All', which is invalid.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: All pens are books. No book is a chair.
Conclusions: I. No pen is a chair.  II. Some books are pens.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Pens lie inside books, which share nothing with chairs, so I follows. II is the valid conversion of 'All pens are books'.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: Some doctors are teachers. All teachers are singers.
Conclusions: I. Some doctors are singers.  II. All singers are doctors.
assumptions-conclusions.e: The doctors who are teachers must be singers, so I follows. Nothing supports II.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: Some cars are buses. Some buses are trucks.
Conclusions: I. Some cars are trucks.  II. All buses are cars.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Two 'some' premises give no definite link between cars and trucks, and II is unsupported.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: No fruit is a vegetable. All apples are fruits.
Conclusions: I. No apple is a vegetable.  II. Some fruits are apples.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Apples lie inside fruits, which exclude vegetables, so I follows. II converts 'All apples are fruits'.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: All engineers are graduates. Some graduates are artists.
Conclusions: I. Some engineers are artists.  II. Some artists are graduates.
assumptions-conclusions.e: The artist-graduates need not be engineers, so I fails. II simply converts 'Some graduates are artists'.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: No man is a bird. Some birds are swans.
Conclusions: I. Some swans are not men.  II. No swan is a man.
assumptions-conclusions.e: The swans that are birds cannot be men, so I follows. Swans that are not birds are unknown, so II does not.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statements: All roads are rivers. Some rivers are mountains. No mountain is a valley.
Conclusions: I. Some rivers are not valleys.  II. Some roads are mountains.
assumptions-conclusions.e: The rivers that are mountains cannot be valleys, so I follows. The mountain-rivers need not be roads.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A notice from the city transport office reads: 'Travel by metro to avoid traffic jams.'
Assumptions: I. The metro is not affected by road traffic jams.  II. Everyone in the city owns a car.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The advice only makes sense if the metro escapes road traffic. Car ownership is irrelevant.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: 'If you want to improve your English, read a newspaper daily,' says a teacher.
Assumptions: I. Reading newspapers can help improve English.  II. Newspapers are written only in English.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The advice presumes reading helps. It does not assume that every newspaper is in English.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The government will give free textbooks to all children in government schools.
Assumptions: I. Some parents find it hard to buy textbooks.  II. Children in private schools do not need textbooks.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: Free books presume a need. Nothing is assumed about private-school children.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A railway advertisement says, 'Book your tickets early to get a confirmed seat.'
Assumptions: I. Seats may get filled up later.  II. Tickets can be booked in advance.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The advice assumes seats can run out and that advance booking is possible.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The company has asked employees to work from home on Fridays to save electricity.
Assumptions: I. Running the office uses a significant amount of electricity.  II. Employees can do their work from home.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The saving presumes the office uses notable power, and the order presumes the work can be done from home.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A sign in an office building reads: 'Do not use the lift in case of fire.'
Assumptions: I. The lift may become unsafe during a fire.  II. There is another way, such as stairs, to leave the building.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The warning assumes the lift is risky in a fire and that people have another exit.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The library will remain open till 10 p.m. during the exam season.
Assumptions: I. Students may want to study in the library late in the evening.  II. The library has no staff after 6 p.m.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: Longer hours presume demand. II would make late opening impossible, so it is not assumed.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A shopkeeper puts up a board: 'No credit. Cash only.'
Assumptions: I. Some customers ask to buy on credit.  II. All customers carry enough cash.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The board exists because credit is requested. It does not assume every customer has enough cash.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A minister says, 'We will cut the fuel price only if the international crude price falls.'
Assumptions: I. The international crude price affects the domestic fuel price.  II. The international crude price will certainly fall soon.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: Linking the two prices assumes I. The statement makes no prediction, so II is not assumed.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A traffic notice says, 'Wear a helmet while riding a two-wheeler.'
Assumptions: I. Every rider already wears a helmet.  II. Helmets can reduce the risk of head injury.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The notice assumes helmets protect riders. If everyone already wore one, no notice would be needed.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The bank has introduced a mobile app for opening accounts.
Assumptions: I. All customers prefer visiting the branch.  II. Many customers have access to smartphones.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: Launching an app assumes customers can use it. I would make the app pointless.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Rahul tells his friend, 'Join the coaching class near the station if you want to crack the exam.'
Assumptions: I. The coaching class is the only way to crack the exam.  II. The coaching class helps students prepare for the exam.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The advice assumes the class helps; it does not claim it is the only way.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The municipality has warned residents not to drink tap water without boiling it.
Assumptions: I. Boiling can make the water safe to drink.  II. Residents have the means to boil water.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The warning assumes boiling works and that residents can follow the instruction.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The principal cancelled the annual sports day because of the heat wave.
Assumptions: I. The heat wave could harm students playing outdoors.  II. The students do not like sports.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: The stated reason assumes heat is harmful. Nothing suggests students dislike sports.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Ravi bought a new laptop last week.
Assumptions: I. Ravi's old laptop had stopped working.  II. Laptops are cheaper now than last year.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: A purchase can have many reasons; neither assumption is necessary.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The train to Delhi is running two hours late.
Assumptions: I. The train will be cancelled.  II. All trains are running late today.
o: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
assumptions-conclusions.e: A delay does not imply cancellation, and one late train says nothing about all trains.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Many students in a school failed in mathematics this year.
Courses of action: I. The school should arrange remedial classes in mathematics.  II. Mathematics should be removed from the syllabus.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Remedial classes address the problem. Removing the subject is impractical and avoids it.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: There is a sudden outbreak of dengue in a locality.
Courses of action: I. The municipality should spray anti-mosquito chemicals in the area.  II. Residents should be told how to stop water collecting around their homes.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Both actions target the mosquitoes that spread dengue.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A large number of railway passengers travel without tickets.
Courses of action: I. Ticket checking should be made more frequent.  II. All trains should be stopped until the problem is solved.
assumptions-conclusions.e: More checks are a practical remedy; stopping all trains is extreme.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A bridge has developed cracks after heavy rains.
Courses of action: I. Traffic on the bridge should be stopped until it is inspected.  II. Engineers should examine the bridge and suggest repairs.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Stopping traffic ensures safety and inspection leads to repair; both follow.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Some employees of an office often arrive late.
Courses of action: I. All employees should be dismissed.  II. The office should close an hour later every day.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Dismissing everyone is extreme, and closing later does not address late arrival.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Prices of onions have risen sharply due to crop damage.
Courses of action: I. The government should release onions from its buffer stock.  II. People should be banned from eating onions.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Releasing stock increases supply and eases prices. A ban is absurd.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: A survey shows many rural children drop out of school to work on farms.
Courses of action: I. The government should offer incentives such as free meals to keep children in school.  II. Farming should be banned in rural areas.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Incentives tackle the cause directly. Banning farming is impractical.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: The museum is open on all days except Monday.
Conclusions: I. The museum is open on Sunday.  II. The museum is closed on Monday.
assumptions-conclusions.e: 'All days except Monday' means open on Sunday and closed on Monday.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Only students with 75% attendance can sit the final exam. Raj has 60% attendance.
Conclusions: I. Raj cannot sit the final exam.  II. Raj is a poor student.
assumptions-conclusions.e: Raj falls below the required attendance, so I follows. Attendance says nothing about ability.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Of all the shops on this street, only Ravi's shop sells imported chocolates.
Conclusions: I. No other shop on this street sells imported chocolates.  II. Ravi's shop sells only imported chocolates.
assumptions-conclusions.e: 'Only Ravi's shop' excludes other shops, so I follows. It does not limit what Ravi's shop sells.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Most of the students who took the coaching class passed the exam.
Conclusions: I. All students who passed the exam took the coaching class.  II. Some students who took the coaching class did not pass.
assumptions-conclusions.e: 'Most' does not rule out 'all', so II is not certain, and nothing is said about students who skipped the class.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: All employees of the firm got a bonus this year. Mohan did not get a bonus.
Conclusions: I. Mohan is not an employee of the firm.  II. The firm made a loss this year.
assumptions-conclusions.e: If Mohan were an employee he would have got a bonus, so I follows. Paying bonuses suggests no loss, so II does not follow.

assumptions-conclusions.p:
Statement: Every member of the club is above 18 years of age. Tina is a member of the club.
Conclusions: I. Tina is above 18.  II. Tina is the youngest member.
assumptions-conclusions.e: I follows directly from the rule. Nothing indicates Tina's rank by age.

seating-arrangement.p: Five friends P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row facing north. Q is at the extreme right. P is third from the left. S is immediately to the left of Q. R is not adjacent to P. Who is at the extreme left?
seating-arrangement.e: Q = 5th, S = 4th, P = 3rd. R and T fill 1st and 2nd. R cannot be next to P, so R = 1st.

seating-arrangement.p: Six people A, B, C, D, E, F sit around a circular table facing the centre. A sits opposite D. B is immediately to the right of A. C sits opposite F. Who sits opposite B?
seating-arrangement.e: Number seats clockwise 1–6 with A = 1, D = 4. Facing the centre, B on A's right is seat 6. C and F take 2 and 5, so E is seat 3, opposite B.

seating-arrangement.p: Five people A, B, C, D and E sit in a row facing north. B sits immediately between A and C. D is at the right end. E is not at the left end. Who sits second from the left?
seating-arrangement.e: D is 5th. The block A-B-C (either way) cannot start at 2nd (E would be 1st), so it occupies 1st–3rd and E is 4th. B is 2nd.

seating-arrangement.p: Four friends P, Q, R and S sit around a circular table facing the centre. P sits opposite R. Q is immediately to the left of P. Who sits immediately to the right of P?
seating-arrangement.e: P and R are opposite; Q and S fill the other two seats. Q is on P's left, so S is on P's right.

seating-arrangement.p: Seven people A–G sit in a row facing north. F is at the left end, B is immediately left of C, and C is third from the left. A is 5th, G is at the right end, and D sits between C and A. Who sits between A and G?
seating-arrangement.e: Order: F, B, C, D, A, E, G. E sits between A and G.

seating-arrangement.p: In a row of 40 students, Ravi is 12th from the left. What is his position from the right?
seating-arrangement.e: Position from right = 40 − 12 + 1 = 29.

seating-arrangement.p: Eight people sit in a row. Ayan is 3rd from the left and Beena is 4th from the right. How many people sit between them?
seating-arrangement.e: Beena is 8 − 4 + 1 = 5th from the left. Between the 3rd and 5th there is 1 person.

seating-arrangement.p: Five people stand in a queue. P is ahead of Q but behind R. S is behind Q. T is ahead of R. Who is in the third position from the front?
seating-arrangement.e: Order: T, R, P, Q, S. The third is P.

seating-arrangement.p: Four people A, B, C and D sit in a row facing north. A is left of B. C is right of B. D is left of A. Who is at the extreme left?
seating-arrangement.e: The order is D, A, B, C.

seating-arrangement.p: Five people sit in a row. P is in the middle. Q sits immediately to the left of P and R immediately to the right of P. Which two positions remain for S and T?
w: Both seats to the left of P
Both seats to the right of P
seating-arrangement.e: P occupies seat 3, Q seat 2 and R seat 4, leaving seats 1 and 5 for S and T.

seating-arrangement.p: Six people sit around a circular table facing the centre. A sits opposite D. B sits opposite E. Which person sits opposite C?
seating-arrangement.e: Opposite pairs are A-D, B-E, and the remaining pair C-F.

seating-arrangement.p: Seven people stand in a line. M is fourth from the left. What is M's position from the right?
seating-arrangement.e: Position from right = 7 − 4 + 1 = 4.

seating-arrangement.p: In a row of 25 people, R is 9th from the left. What is R's position from the right?
In a row facing north, A sits immediately left of B, and B sits immediately left of C. Who sits in the middle of these three?
seating-arrangement.e: The order is A-B-C from left to right, so the second person is in the middle.

seating-arrangement.p: Four people P, Q, R and S sit in a row. P is at the far left, S at the far right, and Q sits immediately to the right of P. Who sits immediately to the left of S?
seating-arrangement.e: The only order is P-Q-R-S.

seating-arrangement.p: In a row of 30 people, Kiran is 8th from the right. What is her position from the left?
seating-arrangement.e: Position from the left = 30 − 8 + 1 = 23.

seating-arrangement.p: A, B and C sit in a row facing north. B is to the left of C, and A is to the right of C. Who is in the middle?
seating-arrangement.e: From left to right the order is B, C, A, so C is in the middle.

seating-arrangement.p: Four friends sit in a row facing north. P is at the right end and Q at the left end. R sits to the left of S. Who is second from the left?
seating-arrangement.e: Q and P take the ends; R must be left of S in the middle seats: Q, R, S, P.

seating-arrangement.p: A, B, C and D sit around a square table, one on each side, facing the centre. A is opposite B, and C is to the left of A. Who is to the right of A?
seating-arrangement.e: A's two neighbours are C and D. C is on A's left, so D is on A's right.

seating-arrangement.p: Five students stand in a line facing north. O is at the left end and Q at the right end. P is immediately left of N, and M is immediately right of N. Who is in the middle?
seating-arrangement.e: P, N, M fill the three middle places in that order, so N is third: O, P, N, M, Q.

seating-arrangement.p: Eight friends sit in a row facing north. Anil is 3rd from the left, and Bina is second to the right of Anil. What is Bina's position from the right?
seating-arrangement.e: Bina is 5th from the left, so from the right she is 8 − 5 + 1 = 4th.

seating-arrangement.p: Seven people sit in a row facing north. D is in the exact middle and E is third to the right of D. Where does E sit?
seating-arrangement.e: D is 4th from the left, so E is 4 + 3 = 7th: the right end.

seating-arrangement.p: In a row of 21 boys, Amit is exactly in the middle. What is Amit's position from the left?
seating-arrangement.e: With 10 boys on each side, Amit is (21 + 1) ÷ 2 = 11th.

seating-arrangement.p: Six chairs stand in a row. Sam sits 2nd from the left and Tom 2nd from the right. How many chairs are between them?
seating-arrangement.e: Sam is in chair 2 and Tom in chair 5, leaving chairs 3 and 4 between them.

seating-arrangement.p: Four people sit around a circular table facing the centre. A is opposite C, and B is to the right of A. Who is to the left of A?
seating-arrangement.e: A's neighbours are B and D. B is on A's right, so D is on A's left.

seating-arrangement.p: Ten people sit in a row facing north. Asha is 4th from the left, and Bela, to Asha's right, has 3 people between them. What is Bela's position from the right?
seating-arrangement.e: Bela is 4 + 4 = 8th from the left, so from the right she is 10 − 8 + 1 = 3rd.

seating-arrangement.p: In a row of girls, Rani is 9th from the left and Sita 6th from the right. When they swap places, Rani becomes 15th from the left. How many girls are in the row?
seating-arrangement.e: Rani now occupies Sita's place, which is 15th from the left and 6th from the right: 15 + 6 − 1 = 20.

seating-arrangement.p: In a queue, Tarun is 10th from the front and Varun 12th from the back. There are 4 people between them, and Tarun is ahead. How many people are in the queue?
seating-arrangement.e: Varun is 10 + 4 + 1 = 15th from the front and 12th from the back: 15 + 12 − 1 = 26.

seating-arrangement.p: Five cars are parked in a line, numbered 1–5 from the left. Red is in the middle and Green immediately right of Red. Blue is at an end next to White. Where is the Black car?
seating-arrangement.e: Red = 3, Green = 4. Blue at 5 would need White at 4, which is taken, so Blue = 1 and White = 2, leaving Black at 5.

seating-arrangement.p: Six friends A–F sit in a row facing north, with A at the left end and B at the right end. C sits next to A and D next to B. E sits immediately left of F. Who is fourth from the left?
seating-arrangement.e: A, C, _, _, D, B. E and F fill seats 3 and 4 with E on the left, so F is 4th.

seating-arrangement.p: Five people P, Q, R, S, T sit in a row facing south. R is at the right end and T third from the left. Q is immediately right of P. S is immediately left of R. Who is at the left end?
seating-arrangement.e: Counting from their own left: R = 5, T = 3, S = 4. P and Q take seats 1 and 2 with Q to P's right, so P is at the left end.

seating-arrangement.p: Six people sit around a circular table facing the centre. A is opposite B. C is immediately right of A, and D immediately right of B. E sits next to D. Who sits opposite C?
seating-arrangement.e: Seats 1–6 clockwise: A = 1, B = 4. Facing the centre, the right neighbour is anticlockwise, so C = 6 and D = 3. E next to D takes 2, F takes 5. Seat 3 (D) is opposite C.

seating-arrangement.p: Five friends sit around a circular table facing the centre. Ravi sits between Sunil and Tarun. Uma is immediately left of Sunil, and Vijay immediately right of Tarun. Who sits between Uma and Tarun?
seating-arrangement.e: Going clockwise (each person's left): Ravi, Sunil, Uma, then the last two seats. Vijay must be on Tarun's right, giving Ravi, Sunil, Uma, Vijay, Tarun. Vijay sits between Uma and Tarun.

seating-arrangement.p: A, B, C sit in a row facing north, and D, E, F sit in a row facing south directly opposite them. B is in the middle of its row, E faces B, A is at the west end, and F is diagonally opposite A. Who faces A?
seating-arrangement.e: The north-facing row is A, B, C from west to east. E is opposite B, and F is diagonal to A, so F is at the east end; D is at the west end, facing A.

seating-arrangement.p: Seven people sit in a row facing north. G is fourth from the left, H second to the left of G, and J at the right end. How many people sit between H and J?
seating-arrangement.e: H is in seat 2 and J in seat 7, so seats 3–6 (4 people) lie between them.

seating-arrangement.p: Eight people sit around a circular table facing the centre. P is opposite Q. R is second to the right of P, and S is opposite R. How many people sit between Q and S along the shorter side?
seating-arrangement.e: Seats 1–8 clockwise: P = 1, Q = 5. Rightwards is anticlockwise, so R = 7 and S = 3. Only seat 4 lies between S and Q.

seating-arrangement.p: Six people A–F sit in a row facing north. C is second from the right, and A immediately left of C. B is at the left end and D at the right end. E is not next to B. Who is second from the left?
seating-arrangement.e: B = 1, A = 4, C = 5, D = 6. E cannot be in seat 2 (next to B), so E = 3 and F = 2.

seating-arrangement.p: Five people sit in a row facing north. Q is left of T but right of S. P is right of T, and R is left of S. Who is in the middle?
seating-arrangement.e: The order is R, S, Q, T, P, so Q is in the middle.

seating-arrangement.p: Nine people sit in a row facing north. X is fifth from the left, Y third to the right of X, and Z second to the left of Y. What is Z's position from the right end?
seating-arrangement.e: X = 5, Y = 8, Z = 6 from the left, so Z is 9 − 6 + 1 = 4th from the right.

seating-arrangement.p: Eight friends A–H sit around a circular table facing the centre. A is third to the left of B. C is opposite A. D is second to the right of C. E is opposite D. F is immediately right of A. G is adjacent to C. Who sits between D and A?
seating-arrangement.e: Seats 1–8 clockwise, left = clockwise: B = 1, A = 4, C = 8, D = 6, E = 2, F = 3. G next to C takes 7, so H = 5, between D and A.

seating-arrangement.p: Six people P–U sit around a circular table facing the centre. P is opposite S. Q is second to the left of P. R is immediately left of S. T is not adjacent to Q. Who is opposite T?
seating-arrangement.e: Seats 1–6 clockwise, left = clockwise: P = 1, S = 4, Q = 3, R = 5. T and U take 2 and 6; seat 2 touches Q, so T = 6, opposite seat 3 (Q).

seating-arrangement.p: Five people A–E sit in a row facing north. A is at the right end. Exactly one person sits between A and B. D is immediately right of B. C is at an end, and E is not. Who is in the middle?
seating-arrangement.e: A = 5, B = 3, D = 4. C takes the other end (1) and E sits 2nd. B is in the middle.

seating-arrangement.p: Seven people A–G sit in a row facing north. B and E are at the two ends. F is third to the right of B, and A immediately right of F. G is immediately left of E. C is not next to F. Who sits immediately right of D?
seating-arrangement.e: F is right of B, so B = 1, F = 4, A = 5, E = 7, G = 6. C cannot be in seat 3 (next to F), so C = 2 and D = 3, with F on D's right.

seating-arrangement.p: Four friends sit around a square table, one on each side. P and R face the centre; Q and S face outward. Q is to the right of P. Who is to the right of Q?
seating-arrangement.e: Facing the centre, P's right is his anticlockwise neighbour, Q. Q faces outward, so Q's right is clockwise from Q, which is back to P.

seating-arrangement.p: Row 1 (A, B, C, D) faces south and Row 2 (P, Q, R, S) faces north, each person facing one in the other row. D is at an end; B is second to the right of D; C is at the right end of Row 1; Q faces B; S faces A; R is at the left end of Row 2. Who faces D?
seating-arrangement.e: Number seats 1–4 west to east. South-facers' right is west, so D = 4, B = 2, C = 1, A = 3. North-facers' left is west, so R = 1; Q = 2, S = 3, P = 4 faces D.

seating-arrangement.p: Seven people J–P sit in a row facing north. M is in the middle. Two people sit between J and M. K is immediately right of J. P is at an end, not next to J. N is second to the left of O. Who sits between O and P?
seating-arrangement.e: M = 4. J is 1 or 7, but K is right of J, so J = 1, K = 2, P = 7. N and O take 3 and 5, leaving L = 6, between O and P.

seating-arrangement.p: Eight people A–H sit around a circular table facing the centre. B is second to the left of A. C is opposite B. D is immediately left of C. E is opposite A. F is not adjacent to A. G is second to the right of H. Who sits between B and E?
seating-arrangement.e: Seats clockwise, left = clockwise: A = 1, B = 3, C = 7, D = 8, E = 5. Seats 2, 4, 6 remain; G = H − 2 allows (H4, G2) or (H6, G4), and only the first keeps F off seat 2. So H = 4, between B and E.

seating-arrangement.p: Rahul, Sohan, Tina, Uday, Vivek and Wasim sit around a circular table facing the centre. Rahul is opposite Sohan. Tina sits between Rahul and Uday. Vivek is immediately left of Sohan. Who sits opposite Tina?
seating-arrangement.e: Seats clockwise, left = clockwise: Rahul = 1, Sohan = 4, Vivek = 5. Tina at 6 would need Uday at 5, so Tina = 2, Uday = 3, Wasim = 6. Seat 5 (Vivek) is opposite Tina.

seating-arrangement.p: Six people A–F sit in a row facing north. A is not at an end. B is second to the right of A. C is immediately left of D, who is at the right end. E is not next to B. Who is at the left end?
seating-arrangement.e: D = 6, C = 5. B = A + 2 must avoid 5 and 6, so A = 2, B = 4. E cannot be in seat 3, so E = 1 and F = 3.

seating-arrangement.p: Seven friends sit around a circular table facing the centre. Asha is immediately left of Bina. Chitra is third to the right of Asha. Deepa sits between Bina and Chitra. Esha is second to the left of Asha. Gita is not next to Asha, and Farah fills the last seat. Who is immediately right of Esha?
seating-arrangement.e: Seats 1–7 clockwise, left = clockwise: Bina = 1, Asha = 2, Chitra = 6, Deepa = 7, Esha = 4. Gita cannot take 3, so Gita = 5 and Farah = 3, which is Esha's right.

w: Honesty always is best the policy
Always honesty the is best policy
The honesty is always best policy
ordering-words.e: Subject (Honesty), verb (is), adverb (always), then the noun phrase (the best policy).

w: Never you should judge by a book its cover
You never should a book judge by its cover
Judge you should never a book by cover its
ordering-words.e: The proverb starts with the subject and the modal 'should', then the adverb 'never'.
