ordering-words.c: The meeting has been postponed until tomorrow
w: The meeting been has postponed until tomorrow
Has the meeting been until postponed tomorrow
The has meeting been postponed tomorrow until
ordering-words.e: Subject + auxiliary (has been) + participle + time phrase.

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: working / she / has / here / for / years / been / five

w: She has working been here for five years
She been has working here five for years
Here she has been working for years five
ordering-words.e: Present perfect continuous: has been working, followed by place and duration.

w: I my forgot umbrella at home
Forgot I my at home umbrella
I forgot at home my umbrella
ordering-words.e: Subject, verb, object (my umbrella), then place.

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: is / all / not / that / glitters / gold
ordering-words.c: All that glitters is not gold
w: That all glitters is not gold
All glitters that not is gold
Not all that is glitters gold
ordering-words.e: The proverb: All (that glitters) is not gold.

ordering-words.c: I want to learn how to swim
w: I to want learn how to swim
I want learn to how to swim
Want I to learn how swim to
ordering-words.e: Subject, verb 'want', then the infinitive chain: to learn how to swim.

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: capital / of / is / city / the / large / a / country
ordering-words.c: The capital of the country is a large city
w: The capital is of the country a large city
Capital the of country the is large a city
The country capital a large city of is
ordering-words.e: Noun phrase (the capital of the country), verb (is), complement (a large city).

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: important / is / time / very / management
ordering-words.e: The sentence uses subject + verb + adverb + adjective.

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: completed / before / report / the / deadline / was / the

w: Before the report deadline completed was the
The deadline was before completed the report
Report the was completed deadline before the
ordering-words.e: Start with the subject, then passive verb phrase, followed by the time phrase.

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: if / hard / you / succeed / work / will / you
ordering-words.c: If you work hard, you will succeed
w: You will if succeed work hard you
Work you hard if will succeed you
If hard work you succeed will you
ordering-words.e: The conditional clause comes first, followed by the result clause.

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: never / too / learning / late / is / it / to / start
ordering-words.c: It is never too late to start learning
w: Never it is learning late too start to
It too late is never start learning to
To start is it never learning too late
ordering-words.e: The sentence begins with 'It is', then the expression 'never too late', followed by the infinitive phrase.

ordering-words.p: Arrange the words into a correct sentence: because / cancelled / was / rain / the / match / of / heavy
ordering-words.c: The match was cancelled because of heavy rain
w: Because heavy rain match the cancelled was of
The rain was because of match cancelled heavy
Match the cancelled heavy because of rain was

ordering-sentences.p:
P: He was tired after a long day at work.
Q: He reached home at nine in the evening.
R: So he went straight to bed.
S: Rohan left the office late that day.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: S introduces him leaving; Q he reaches home; P explains he was tired; R the result.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The water began to boil.
Q: She poured the tea into two cups.
R: Meera put the kettle on the stove.
S: She then added the tea leaves to the boiling water.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Kettle on → water boils → 'then added… to the boiling water' → pour.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: However, the team did not give up.
Q: The match began badly for the home side.
R: They scored twice in the last ten minutes.
S: They were two goals down at half-time.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Bad start → worse at half-time → 'However…' → comeback.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Therefore, regular exercise is essential.
Q: Modern jobs keep most people sitting for hours.
R: This lack of movement leads to many health problems.
S: Even a thirty-minute daily walk helps.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Problem → effect → conclusion ('Therefore') → small solution.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The seed sprouts into a small plant.
Q: A farmer sows a seed in the soil.
R: Rain and sunlight help it grow.
S: In time the plant bears fruit.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Chronological: sow → sprout → grow → fruit.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Finally, the bridge opened to traffic.
Q: Engineers surveyed the river for months.
R: Construction started after the design was approved.
S: A design was then prepared.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Survey → design ('then prepared') → construction → opening ('Finally').

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The results were announced the next week.
Q: Students prepared for the examination.
R: They took the examination on Monday.
S: The school issued the timetable a month earlier.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: The timetable is issued, students prepare, they take the exam, and results follow.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: As a result, the road became slippery.
Q: It had been raining heavily for hours.
R: Drivers reduced their speed.
S: Several puddles formed on the road.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Heavy rain causes puddles; the road becomes slippery, prompting drivers to slow down.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The team reviewed the feedback.
Q: They released an updated version.
R: Users reported several issues.
S: The developers fixed the reported problems.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Users report issues, the team reviews feedback, developers fix issues, and an updated version is released.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The plants began to wilt.
Q: The gardener watered them thoroughly.
R: The weather remained hot for several days.
S: After a while, the plants recovered.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Prolonged heat leads to wilting, watering follows, and the plants recover.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Then she mixed the ingredients and baked the cake.
Q: Her mother was delighted when she saw it.
R: She bought flour, sugar and eggs from the market.
S: Riya wanted to bake a cake for her mother's birthday.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: S states the aim, R buys the ingredients, P bakes ('Then'), and Q gives the reaction.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: After a quick bath, he had breakfast.
Q: He then left for college.
R: Arjun switched it off and got out of bed.
S: The alarm rang at six in the morning.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Alarm (S) → 'it' refers to the alarm (R) → bath and breakfast (P) → leaving (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: It found a pot with a little water at the bottom.
Q: It dropped pebbles into the pot one by one.
R: The water rose, and the crow drank it.
S: A thirsty crow was looking for water.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: S introduces the crow, P finds the pot, Q drops pebbles into 'the pot', and R is the result.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: A week later, she was called for an interview.
Q: She performed well and got the job.
R: She sent her application the same day.
S: Meena saw an advertisement for a job.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Advertisement (S) → application (R) → interview a week later (P) → result (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Soon, it began to rain heavily.
Q: The streets were flooded within an hour.
R: Schools declared a holiday for the next day.
S: The sky grew dark with clouds.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Clouds (S) → rain ('Soon', P) → flooding (Q) → holiday as a consequence (R).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Two days later, the conductor found it.
Q: The wallet was returned to Ravi with all his money.
R: He reported the loss at the depot.
S: Ravi lost his wallet on the bus.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Loss (S) → report (R) → found two days later (P) → returned (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Next, select the item you want to buy.
Q: Then, enter your delivery address.
R: Finally, make the payment to place the order.
S: First, open the app and log in.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: The markers First (S), Next (P), Then (Q) and Finally (R) fix the order.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The crop grew well through the winter.
Q: In spring, he harvested a rich crop.
R: He sowed wheat seeds after the first rain.
S: The farmer ploughed his field.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Ploughing (S) → sowing (R) → growth (P) → harvest (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: At first, she found the exercises tiring.
Q: By June, she could run five kilometres easily.
R: Gradually, her stamina improved.
S: Sunita joined a gym in January.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Joining (S) → 'At first' (P) → 'Gradually' (R) → 'By June' (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Everyone left the building by the stairs.
Q: They put out the fire before it spread.
R: The fire brigade arrived within minutes.
S: The fire alarm went off in the office.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Alarm (S) → evacuation (P) → fire brigade arrives (R) → 'They' put out the fire (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The mechanic found that the battery was faulty.
Q: He replaced it, and the phone worked again.
R: He took it to a repair shop.
S: Ankit's phone stopped working.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Problem (S) → repair shop (R) → diagnosis (P) → fix (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The students quickly revised their notes.
Q: Most students found it easier than they expected.
R: The test began at ten o'clock.
S: The teacher announced a surprise test.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Announcement (S) → revision (P) → test begins (R) → reaction (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: When it boils, tea leaves are added.
Q: Milk and sugar are then mixed in.
R: The tea is strained and served hot.
S: Water is heated in a kettle.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Heating (S) → 'When it boils' (P) → 'then' milk and sugar (Q) → serving (R).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: He asked a shopkeeper for directions.
Q: With its help, he found his hotel.
R: The shopkeeper drew a small map for him.
S: A tourist got lost in the old city.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: S sets up the problem, P introduces the shopkeeper, R the map, and 'its help' in Q refers to the map.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: She watered it every day.
Q: Years later, it grew into a big tree.
R: Now it gives her sweet mangoes every summer.
S: Priya planted a mango sapling in her garden.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Planting (S) → care (P) → 'Years later' (Q) → 'Now' (R).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Within a month, the first stock was sold out.
Q: The company then increased production.
R: Its low price attracted many buyers.
S: The company launched a new phone in March.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Launch (S) → 'Its low price' (R) → sold out (P) → 'then' more production (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: He had no money left for a taxi.
Q: His father came and picked him up.
R: So he called his father.
S: Rahul missed the last bus home.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Problem (S) → no taxi money (P) → 'So' he called (R) → father arrives (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:

Q: India won the match by 60 runs.
R: Chasing the target, the visitors lost early wickets.
S: The cricket match started at two o'clock.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Start (S) → first innings (P) → the chase (R) → result (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: She practised for an hour every evening.
Q: After a year, she performed at her school concert.
R: She found a teacher near her house.
S: Neha decided to learn the guitar.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Decision (S) → teacher (R) → practice (P) → 'After a year' (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The envelope is stamped and posted.
Q: A postman delivers it to the receiver.
R: The post office sorts it by address.
S: A letter is written and put in an envelope.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Writing (S) → posting (P) → sorting (R) → delivery (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: This blocks drains and pollutes the soil.
Q: Therefore, people should reduce their use of plastic.
R: Most of it ends up in drains and landfills.
S: Plastic waste is a growing problem in cities.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Problem (S) → where 'it' goes (R) → 'This' effect (P) → 'Therefore' conclusion (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: However, luck alone rarely makes anyone successful.
Q: Luck only helps those who are already prepared.
R: Hard work and planning matter far more.
S: Many people think that success depends on luck.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: A common view (S) is countered by 'However' (P), followed by the real factors (R) and a closing thought (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Earlier, people had to visit stores to buy things.
Q: As a result, many small shops have started selling online too.
R: Now, they can order almost anything from home.
S: The Internet has changed the way we shop.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: General claim (S) → 'Earlier' (P) → 'Now' (R) → 'As a result' (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: They release the oxygen we breathe.
Q: They also provide shelter to countless birds and animals.
R: Hence, cutting trees without replanting is harmful.
S: Trees are vital for life on Earth.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Claim (S) → first reason (P) → 'also' second reason (Q) → 'Hence' conclusion (R).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Children who read regularly also do better at school.
Q: Parents should therefore encourage their children to read.
R: It improves vocabulary and imagination.
S: Reading is a habit worth building early.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Claim (S) → benefit (R) → further benefit with 'also' (P) → 'therefore' advice (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The aim is to help them buy better seeds and tools.
Q: Experts believe this will raise farm incomes.
R: Under it, farmers will get loans at low interest.
S: The government announced a new scheme for farmers.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Announcement (S) → 'Under it' (R) → purpose (P) → expert view (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: It strengthens the heart and muscles.
Q: Besides, it reduces stress and improves mood.
R: That is why doctors recommend at least thirty minutes of activity a day.
S: Exercise is good for both body and mind.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Claim (S) → physical benefit (P) → 'Besides' mental benefit (Q) → 'That is why' (R).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Others, such as trans fats, raise the risk of heart disease.
Q: The key, therefore, is to choose fats wisely rather than avoid them.
R: Some, like those in nuts and fish, actually protect the heart.
S: Not all fats are bad for health.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: S makes the claim; 'Some' (R) and 'Others' (P) split fats into two groups; 'therefore' (Q) concludes.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: This barter system was clumsy, since both sides had to want what the other offered.
Q: Coins were invented to overcome this problem.
R: In early societies, people simply exchanged goods.
S: Money was not always made of paper or metal.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: S opens; R describes barter, which 'This barter system' (P) criticises; 'this problem' in Q points back to P.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: There it performs a 'waggle dance'.
Q: The direction and length of this dance tell other bees where the food is.
R: When a bee finds food, it returns to the hive.
S: The honeybee is a remarkable communicator.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Topic (S) → return to the hive (R) → 'There' = the hive (P) → 'this dance' (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: That is why farmers continue to live on their slopes.
Q: For them, the risk is the price of rich harvests.
R: Yet the ash they spread makes the surrounding soil very fertile.
S: Volcanoes are often seen only as destroyers.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Common view (S) → 'Yet' contrast (R) → 'That is why' (P) → 'For them' = the farmers (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: During sleep, the brain sorts and stores the day's memories.
Q: Cutting sleep to study longer can therefore backfire.
R: This is why students who sleep well often remember more.
S: Sleep is not simply a period of rest.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Claim (S) → mechanism (P) → 'This is why' (R) → 'therefore' conclusion (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Before that, books had to be copied by hand.
Q: The press made books cheaper and spread learning widely.
R: Such books were rare and costly.
S: The printing press was invented in the fifteenth century.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: 'Before that' (P) needs the invention (S); 'Such books' (R) refers to hand-copied books; Q gives the change.

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Only then can she take decisions that people will support.
Q: Such decisions are far more likely to succeed.
R: This allows her to understand the real problems of the team.
S: A good leader listens before speaking.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Claim (S) → 'This' = listening (R) → 'Only then' (P) → 'Such decisions' (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: But they have also made it hard to switch off from work.
Q: Many employees now answer office emails late at night.
R: Some countries have even passed laws giving workers the 'right to disconnect'.
S: Mobile phones have made communication instant.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Benefit (S) → 'But' drawback (P) → example (Q) → 'even' laws in response (R).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Halfway through, he began to feel dizzy.
Q: Instead of quitting, he slowed down and drank water at every stop.
R: On the day of the race, however, it was unusually hot.
S: Rohit had been preparing for the marathon for months.
T: He finished the race, though well behind his target time.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Preparation (S) → 'however' hot day (R) → 'Halfway through' (P) → his response (Q) → the outcome (T).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: The process, however, needs a great deal of energy.
Q: This makes it expensive for poorer countries.
R: It works by removing the salt, usually by forcing water through fine membranes.
S: Cheaper solar-powered plants may solve this problem in future.
T: Desalination turns sea water into drinking water.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Definition (T) → how 'It' works (R) → 'however' drawback (P) → 'This' consequence (Q) → 'this problem' solved (S).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: India then launched Project Tiger to protect them.
Q: Under this project, special tiger reserves were created.
R: By the 1970s, hunting and loss of forests had pushed them close to extinction.
S: Thanks to such efforts, tiger numbers have been rising again.
T: Tigers were once found across most of Asia.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Past range (T) → decline by the 1970s (R) → 'then' Project Tiger (P) → 'this project' (Q) → 'such efforts' (S).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: This is because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day.
Q: Planting trees and using lighter roofs can reduce this effect.
R: They release it slowly at night, keeping temperatures high.
S: Cities are getting hotter than the countryside around them.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Observation (S) → 'This is because' (P) → 'They' = concrete and asphalt (R) → remedy for 'this effect' (Q).

ordering-sentences.p:
P: Research suggests the opposite.
Q: When we switch between tasks, the brain needs time to refocus.
R: These small delays add up, so doing one task at a time is often faster.
S: Most people believe that multitasking saves time.
Choose the correct order.
ordering-sentences.e: Belief (S) → 'the opposite' (P) → reason (Q) → 'These small delays' (R).

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Each of the students (B) have submitted (C) their assignment (D) before the deadline.
spotting-errors.e: 'Each' takes a singular verb: has submitted.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) She do not (B) like to (C) eat (D) spicy food.
spotting-errors.e: Third person singular needs 'does not'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Neither of the two answers (B) are (C) correct (D) in this case.
spotting-errors.e: 'Neither' is singular: 'is'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) He is (B) senior than (C) me (D) by two years.
spotting-errors.e: 'Senior' takes 'to', not 'than': senior to me.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) I have been (B) working here (C) since five years (D) now.
spotting-errors.e: A period of time takes 'for': for five years.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The news (B) that he won (C) were (D) a pleasant surprise.
spotting-errors.e: 'News' is uncountable and singular: was.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Hardly had he reached the station (B) than the train (C) started (D) moving.
spotting-errors.e: 'Hardly' pairs with 'when', not 'than'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) He gave me (B) several informations (C) about the (D) new policy.
spotting-errors.e: 'Information' is uncountable: several pieces of information.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) If I would have (B) known the answer, (C) I would have (D) told you.
spotting-errors.e: Third conditional: if I had known.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The teacher, (B) along with her students, (C) are going (D) on a trip.
spotting-errors.e: The subject is 'teacher'; 'along with…' does not make it plural: is going.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) She is good (B) in mathematics (C) and fond (D) of music.
spotting-errors.e: The correct collocation is 'good at'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) One of my friends (B) are (C) a doctor (D) in London.
spotting-errors.e: 'One of …' takes a singular verb: is.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Neither the players (B) nor the coach (C) were present (D) at the meeting.
spotting-errors.e: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'coach': was present.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) She has (B) less books (C) than her (D) younger brother.
spotting-errors.e: 'Books' is countable, so use 'fewer books'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) No sooner had (B) the bell rung (C) when the students (D) left the room.
spotting-errors.e: 'No sooner' pairs with 'than': No sooner had the bell rung than the students left.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) She is one of the (B) best student (C) in her (D) class.
spotting-errors.e: 'One of the' is followed by a plural noun: best students.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The information (B) provided by them (C) are useful (D) for our research.
spotting-errors.e: 'Information' is uncountable and takes a singular verb: is useful.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) My father (B) go to office (C) by bus (D) every day.
spotting-errors.e: A singular subject in the simple present takes 'goes'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The children (B) was playing (C) in the park (D) when it rained.
spotting-errors.e: 'Children' is plural, so the verb must be 'were playing'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) He bought (B) a new furnitures (C) for his (D) living room.
spotting-errors.e: 'Furniture' is uncountable: 'new furniture' or 'a new piece of furniture'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) I have been knowing (B) him (C) since (D) my childhood.
spotting-errors.e: 'Know' is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous: 'I have known him'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The sun (B) rise (C) in the (D) east.
spotting-errors.e: A general truth with a singular subject needs 'rises'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Ravi and his brother (B) is going (C) to the market (D) this evening.
spotting-errors.e: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb: 'are going'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) We discussed about (B) the problem (C) for nearly (D) an hour.
spotting-errors.e: 'Discuss' takes a direct object: 'We discussed the problem'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) He is (B) the most tallest boy (C) in (D) our class.
spotting-errors.e: Double superlative: use 'the tallest boy'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The number of students (B) in the college (C) have increased (D) this year.
spotting-errors.e: 'The number of' is singular and takes 'has increased'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) A number of students (B) was absent (C) from class (D) yesterday.
spotting-errors.e: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb: 'were absent'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Unless you (B) do not work hard, (C) you will not (D) pass the exam.
spotting-errors.e: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so drop 'do not': 'Unless you work hard'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) He told that (B) he would come (C) to the party (D) on Sunday.
spotting-errors.e: 'Tell' needs a person as object: 'He said that' or 'He told me that'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) She returned back (B) from Delhi (C) after spending (D) a week there.
spotting-errors.e: 'Returned' already means came back, so 'back' is redundant.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Each boy and girl (B) were given (C) a prize (D) at the function.
spotting-errors.e: 'Each … and …' is treated as singular: 'was given'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) I look forward (B) to meet you (C) at the conference (D) next week.
spotting-errors.e: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition and takes a gerund: 'to meeting you'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The police (B) has arrested (C) the thief (D) who stole the car.
spotting-errors.e: 'Police' is always plural: 'have arrested'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) I prefer (B) walking (C) than (D) running.
spotting-errors.e: 'Prefer' is followed by 'to', not 'than': prefer walking to running.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) It is (B) high time (C) we leave (D) for the station.
spotting-errors.e: 'It is high time' takes the past tense: 'we left'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Scarcely had (B) we started (C) than it (D) began to rain.
spotting-errors.e: 'Scarcely' pairs with 'when', not 'than'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The cattle (B) is grazing (C) in the (D) field.
spotting-errors.e: 'Cattle' is a plural noun: 'are grazing'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) She is (B) elder than (C) her sister (D) by two years.
spotting-errors.e: 'Elder' is used before a noun (my elder sister), not with 'than'; the comparison needs 'older than'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) He is one of those (B) people who (C) always tries (D) to help others.
spotting-errors.e: 'Who' refers to 'those people' (plural), so the verb is 'try'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Not only the students (B) but also the teacher (C) were (D) late.
spotting-errors.e: With 'not only … but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'teacher': 'was'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The reason why (B) he failed (C) is because (D) he did not study.
spotting-errors.e: 'The reason … is because' is redundant; use 'is that'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Had I known (B) about the strike, (C) I will not have (D) come here.
spotting-errors.e: A past unreal condition takes 'would not have come'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Being a rainy day, (B) we decided (C) to stay (D) at home.
spotting-errors.e: The participle dangles ('we' were not a rainy day); use 'It being a rainy day'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) The committee consists (B) of five members, (C) each of whom (D) have a vote.
spotting-errors.e: 'Each' is singular: 'has a vote'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Ten kilometres (B) are (C) a long distance (D) to walk.
spotting-errors.e: A distance treated as a single amount takes a singular verb: 'is'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Neither he (B) nor I (C) are going (D) to the party.
spotting-errors.e: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'I': 'am going'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Between you and I, (B) this plan (C) will not (D) work.
spotting-errors.e: 'Between' is a preposition and takes the object pronoun: 'between you and me'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) Whom (B) do you think (C) is (D) the best candidate?
spotting-errors.e: The pronoun is the subject of 'is', so it must be 'Who'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) She is (B) more intelligent (C) than any (D) girl in her class.
spotting-errors.e: She is in the class herself, so compare with 'any other girl'.

spotting-errors.p:
Find the part with the error.
(A) He as well as (B) his friends (C) are (D) coming tonight.
spotting-errors.e: 'As well as' does not make the subject plural; the verb agrees with 'He': 'is coming'.

sentence-correction.e: 'Neither' is singular, and 'of' takes a plural noun.

sentence-correction.c: She doesn't know the answer.
sentence-correction.e: 'Doesn't' already carries the third-person -s, so the main verb stays plain.

sentence-correction.c: He suggested that I take a break.
w: He suggested me to take a break.
He suggested me taking a break.
He suggested to me take a break.
sentence-correction.e: 'Suggest' takes a that-clause (or a gerund), not an object + infinitive.

sentence-correction.c: The furniture is old.
sentence-correction.e: 'Furniture' is uncountable and singular.

sentence-correction.c: I have been living here since 2015.
sentence-correction.e: 'Since' needs the present perfect (continuous).

sentence-correction.c: Each of the players was given a medal.
w: Each of the players were given a medal.
Each of the player was given a medal.
Each players was given a medal.
sentence-correction.e: 'Each' is singular and 'of' takes the plural noun.

sentence-correction.c: Despite the rain, we went out.
w: Despite of the rain, we went out.
In spite the rain, we went out.
Despite that rain we went out.
sentence-correction.e: 'Despite' takes no 'of'; 'in spite' needs 'of'.

sentence-correction.c: He is taller than his brother.
w: He is more taller than his brother.
He is tallest than his brother.
He is taller from his brother.
sentence-correction.e: Comparatives use -er without 'more', followed by 'than'.

sentence-correction.c: The teacher told the students to be quiet.
w: The teacher told to the students to be quiet.
The teacher said the students to be quiet.
The teacher told the students being quiet.
sentence-correction.e: 'Tell' takes a direct object and an infinitive.

sentence-correction.c: I wish I were taller.
w: I wish I would be taller.
I wish I was be taller.
sentence-correction.e: A wish about the present uses the subjunctive 'were'.

sentence-correction.c: Hardly had I reached home when it started raining.
w: Hardly I had reached home when it started raining.
Hardly had I reached home than it started raining.
Hardly I reached home than it started raining.
sentence-correction.e: 'Hardly' is followed by inversion and commonly pairs with 'when'.

sentence-correction.c: Each employee must submit his or her form.
w: Each employees must submit their form.
Each employee must submits the form.
Each of employee must submit form.
sentence-correction.e: 'Each employee' is grammatically singular. Singular 'they' is also widely accepted in modern usage when appropriate.

sentence-correction.c: She has fewer responsibilities than I do.
w: She has less responsibilities than I do.
She have fewer responsibilities than I do.
She has few responsibility than I do.
sentence-correction.e: 'Responsibilities' is countable, so 'fewer' is the standard choice.

sentence-correction.c: If I had known, I would have helped you.
w: If I would have known, I would have helped you.
If I knew, I would have helped you yesterday.
If I had knew, I would help you.
sentence-correction.e: The standard third conditional uses 'if + past perfect' and 'would have + past participle'.

sentence-correction.c: The news is encouraging.
sentence-correction.e: 'News' is grammatically singular in standard English.

sentence-correction.p: Select the correct version of: “He has been working here since five years.”
sentence-correction.c: He has been working here for five years.
w: He worked here since five years.
He is working here since five years.
He has worked here from five years.
sentence-correction.e: Use “for” with a duration.

sentence-correction.p: Select the correct version of: “She is one of the best player in the team.”
sentence-correction.c: She is one of the best players in the team.
w: She is the best players in the team.
She is one best player in the team.
She is one of best player in team.
sentence-correction.e: “One of the” is followed by a plural noun.

sentence-correction.p: Select the correct version of: “I prefer tea than coffee.”
sentence-correction.c: I prefer tea to coffee.
w: I prefer more tea than coffee.
I prefer tea over than coffee.
sentence-correction.e: The standard construction is “prefer X to Y”.

sentence-correction.p: Select the correct version of: “He discussed about the issue.”
sentence-correction.c: He discussed the issue.
sentence-correction.e: “Discuss” takes a direct object without “about”.

sentence-correction.c: The children are playing in the garden.
w: The children is playing in the garden.
The childrens are playing in the garden.
The children are play in the garden.
sentence-correction.e: 'Children' is already plural and takes 'are playing'.

sentence-correction.c: He goes to school by bus.
w: He go to school by bus.
He going to school by bus.
He goes to school on bus.
sentence-correction.e: A singular subject takes 'goes', and the fixed phrase is 'by bus'.

sentence-correction.c: There are many books on the table.
w: There is many books on the table.
There are much books on the table.
There are many book on the table.
sentence-correction.e: 'Books' is plural and countable: 'There are many books'.

sentence-correction.c: I have finished my homework.
w: I am finished my homework yesterday.
sentence-correction.e: The present perfect is 'have' + past participle 'finished'.

sentence-correction.c: She sings better than her sister.
w: She sings more better than her sister.
She sings best than her sister.
She sings good than her sister.
sentence-correction.e: The comparative of 'well' is 'better', with no 'more'.

sentence-correction.c: My brother and I went to the market.
w: Me and my brother went to the market.
My brother and me went to the market.
I and my brother goes to the market.
sentence-correction.e: The subject needs the subject pronoun 'I', placed after the other person by convention.

sentence-correction.c: He has two sisters-in-law.
sentence-correction.e: In compound nouns like this, the main noun takes the plural: sisters-in-law.

sentence-correction.c: The scissors are on the table.
w: The scissors is on the table.
The scissor are on the table.
A scissors is on the table.
sentence-correction.e: 'Scissors' is a plural noun and takes 'are'.

sentence-correction.c: Please give me some information about the course.
w: Please give me an information about the course.
Please give me some informations about the course.
Please give me many information about the course.
sentence-correction.e: 'Information' is uncountable: no 'an', no plural, and 'some' rather than 'many'.

sentence-correction.c: One of my friends lives in Pune.
w: One of my friend lives in Pune.
One of my friends live in Pune.
One of my friend live in Pune.
sentence-correction.e: 'One of' takes a plural noun (friends) and a singular verb (lives).

sentence-correction.c: She is good at painting.
sentence-correction.e: The collocation for a skill is 'good at'.

sentence-correction.c: He was accused of theft.
sentence-correction.e: 'Accuse' takes 'of'.

sentence-correction.c: I am looking forward to seeing you.
w: I am looking forward to see you.
I am looking forward for seeing you.
I am looking forward to saw you.
sentence-correction.e: 'Look forward to' is followed by a gerund.

sentence-correction.c: Neither Ram nor his friends were at home.
w: Neither Ram nor his friends was at home.
Neither Ram or his friends were at home.
Neither Ram nor his friends is at home.
sentence-correction.e: 'Neither' pairs with 'nor', and the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'friends'.

sentence-correction.c: The man who called you is my uncle.
w: The man which called you is my uncle.
The man whom called you is my uncle.
The man who called you are my uncle.
sentence-correction.e: Use 'who' for a person acting as subject, and singular 'is' for 'the man'.

sentence-correction.c: She has been ill since Monday.
w: She has been ill from Monday.
sentence-correction.e: A state continuing from a past point takes the present perfect with 'since'.

sentence-correction.c: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train.
w: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the train.
Unless you will hurry, you will miss the train.
Unless you hurried, you will miss the train.
sentence-correction.e: 'Unless' already means 'if not' and takes the present tense for a future condition.

sentence-correction.c: He said that he was tired.
w: He told that he was tired.
He said me that he was tired.
He said to that he was tired.
sentence-correction.e: 'Say' needs no personal object; 'tell' needs one ('told me').

sentence-correction.c: No sooner had he arrived than the meeting began.
w: No sooner had he arrived when the meeting began.
No sooner he had arrived than the meeting began.
No sooner did he arrived than the meeting began.
sentence-correction.e: 'No sooner' takes inversion (had he arrived) and pairs with 'than'.

sentence-correction.c: Mathematics is my favourite subject.
sentence-correction.e: Subject names ending in -ics, like mathematics, are singular.

sentence-correction.c: Had I known about the delay, I would have taken a later train.
w: Had I known about the delay, I will have taken a later train.
If I had knew about the delay, I would have taken a later train.
Had I know about the delay, I would take a later train.
sentence-correction.e: An inverted third conditional: 'Had I known …, I would have + past participle'.

sentence-correction.c: It is high time we left for the airport.
w: It is high time we leave for the airport.
It is high time we will leave for the airport.
It is high time we have left for the airport.
sentence-correction.e: 'It is high time' is followed by the past tense to express urgency.

sentence-correction.c: Not only the players but also the coach was praised.
w: Not only the players but also the coach were praised.
Not only the players but the coach also were praised.
Not only the players but also the coach are praised yesterday.
sentence-correction.e: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the coach': 'was'.

sentence-correction.c: She is more intelligent than any other student in the class.
w: She is more intelligent than any student in the class.
She is most intelligent than any other student in the class.
She is more intelligent than all other student in the class.
sentence-correction.e: She belongs to the class, so the comparison must exclude her: 'any other student'.

sentence-correction.c: The reason he failed is that he did not prepare.
w: The reason he failed is because he did not prepare.
The reason why he failed is due to he did not prepare.
The reason he failed is that he does not prepared.
sentence-correction.e: 'The reason … is that' is the correct form; 'reason … because' is redundant.

sentence-correction.c: Who do you think will win the match?
w: Whom do you think will win the match?
Who do you think will wins the match?
Whom you think will win the match?
sentence-correction.e: The pronoun is the subject of 'will win', so it must be 'who'.

sentence-correction.c: Walking along the beach, I found a shell.
w: Walking along the beach, a shell was found by me.
Walking along the beach, a shell caught my eye.
Walk along the beach, I found a shell.
sentence-correction.e: The opening participle must describe the subject that follows; only 'I' can be walking.

sentence-correction.c: He is one of those people who always help others.
w: He is one of those people who always helps others.
He is one of those people which always help others.
He is one of that people who always help others.
sentence-correction.e: 'Who' refers to 'those people', so the verb is plural: 'help'.

sentence-correction.c: Between you and me, the plan is risky.
w: Between you and I, the plan is risky.
Between you and myself, the plan is risky.
Among you and I, the plan is risky.
sentence-correction.e: 'Between' takes object pronouns: 'you and me'.

sentence-correction.c: The number of accidents has decreased this year.
w: The number of accidents have decreased this year.
A number of accidents has decreased this year.
The number of accident have decreased this year.
sentence-correction.e: 'The number of' is singular and takes 'has'.

sentence-correction.c: Scarcely had we reached the station when the train left.
w: Scarcely had we reached the station than the train left.
Scarcely we had reached the station when the train left.
Scarcely had we reach the station when the train left.
sentence-correction.e: 'Scarcely' takes inversion (had we reached) and pairs with 'when'.

synonyms-antonyms.e: Abundant means existing in large quantities.
Generous gives freely; stingy does not.
Candid means open and honest.
Ancient is very old; modern is of the present.
Diligent means showing steady, careful effort.
To expand is to get bigger; to contract is to get smaller.
Ephemeral lasts only a very short time.
The other three are synonyms of victory.
Obstinate means refusing to change one's mind.
Transparent lets light through; opaque does not.
Benevolent means well-meaning and kindly.
An optimist expects good outcomes; a pessimist expects bad ones.
Meticulous means paying great attention to detail.
Brave means ready to face danger; cowardly means the opposite.
Reluctant means hesitant or unwilling to do something.
Frugal means economical; wasteful is the opposite.
Obsolete means no longer in use or out of date.
Hostile means unfriendly or antagonistic.
Vigilant means alert and watchful.
Ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation; clear is the opposite.
Prudent means showing careful judgment.
To commence is to start or begin.
To arrive is to come; to depart is to leave.
Brief means lasting a short time or using few words.
Humble means modest; arrogant means having an inflated sense of importance.
Enormous means very large.
To accept is to take willingly; to reject is to refuse.
Genuine means real or authentic.
Scarce means in short supply; plentiful is its opposite.
Eloquent means fluent and persuasive in speech.
Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy.
Impartial means treating all sides equally.
To conceal is to hide; to reveal is to make known.
To hinder is to create obstacles.
Futile means producing no result; fruitful means productive.
Lucid means expressed clearly and easy to understand.
Tedious means tiresome and dull.
In jeopardy means in danger of loss or harm.
Gregarious means fond of company.
Loquacious means very talkative; taciturn means saying little.
Pragmatic means dealing with things sensibly and realistically.
Adversity is hardship; prosperity is success and good fortune.
Ubiquitous means found everywhere.
Magnanimous means generous and forgiving; petty means small-minded.
Capricious means given to sudden changes of mood or behaviour.
To ameliorate is to make something better.
To exonerate is to clear someone of blame.
Zenith is the highest point; nadir is the lowest.
Surreptitious means done secretly to avoid notice.
Indigenous means native to a place; foreign means from elsewhere.

fill-blanks.p: He is allergic ___ peanuts.
fill-blanks.e: 'Allergic to' is the fixed collocation.

fill-blanks.p: She is afraid ___ spiders.
fill-blanks.e: 'Afraid of' is the fixed collocation.

fill-blanks.p: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ aware of the change.
fill-blanks.e: With 'neither … nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students'.

fill-blanks.p: If it ___ tomorrow, we will cancel the trip.
fill-blanks.e: First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb.

fill-blanks.p: He has been waiting ___ two hours.
fill-blanks.e: 'For' goes with a duration; 'since' with a starting point.

fill-blanks.p: The thief was caught ___ the act of stealing.
fill-blanks.e: 'Caught in the act' is the idiom.

fill-blanks.p: She spoke so ___ that nobody could hear her.
fill-blanks.e: An adverb is needed to modify 'spoke'.

fill-blanks.p: The meeting was called ___ due to heavy rain.
fill-blanks.e: 'Call off' means to cancel.

fill-blanks.p: I would rather ___ at home than go out in this weather.
fill-blanks.e: 'Would rather' is followed by the bare infinitive.

fill-blanks.p: The more you practise, the ___ you become.
fill-blanks.e: 'The more …, the better …' needs the comparative.

fill-blanks.p: Despite his poverty, he was always ___ to help others.
fill-blanks.e: 'Despite' signals contrast, so a positive trait fits.

fill-blanks.p: The doctor advised him to ___ from smoking.
fill-blanks.e: 'Refrain from' is the correct collocation.

fill-blanks.p: The manager insisted ___ reviewing the report before publication.
fill-blanks.e: 'Insist on' is the standard construction before a noun or gerund.

fill-blanks.p: Neither of the proposals ___ acceptable.
fill-blanks.e: 'Neither' is treated as singular in standard formal usage.

fill-blanks.p: By the time we arrived, the film ___.
fill-blanks.e: The past perfect marks an event completed before another past event.

fill-blanks.p: She is capable ___ solving complex problems.
fill-blanks.e: 'Capable of' is followed by a noun or gerund.

fill-blanks.p: The committee will meet ___ Monday morning.
fill-blanks.e: 'On' is used with days and specific dates.

fill-blanks.p: He would have passed if he ___ harder.
fill-blanks.e: This is a third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

fill-blanks.p: The flight was delayed ___ dense fog.
fill-blanks.e: 'Because of' introduces a noun phrase giving the reason.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: Despite the heavy rain, the match continued ____ interruption.
fill-blanks.e: “Without interruption” means it continued uninterrupted.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The manager asked everyone to ____ the deadline.
fill-blanks.e: 'Meet a deadline' is the standard collocation.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The committee will ____ a decision tomorrow.
fill-blanks.e: The usual collocation is “make a decision”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: He apologized ____ being late.
fill-blanks.e: The correct phrase is “apologize for” an action.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The evidence was not sufficient ____ prove the claim.
fill-blanks.e: The structure is “sufficient to prove”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: Please refrain ____ making unnecessary noise.
fill-blanks.e: The correct phrase is “refrain from”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The new policy will come ____ effect next month.
fill-blanks.e: The expression is “come into effect”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: She succeeded ____ convincing the panel.
fill-blanks.e: The correct phrase is “succeed in doing something”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: He has a strong preference ____ tea.
fill-blanks.e: The standard phrase is “preference for”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The team is looking forward ____ the launch.
fill-blanks.e: “Look forward to” is followed by a noun or gerund.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The suspect was accused ____ theft.
fill-blanks.e: The correct phrase is “accused of”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: Hardly had we arrived ____ the show began.
fill-blanks.e: The correlative construction is “hardly…when”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: No sooner had she left ____ it started raining.
fill-blanks.e: The correlative construction is “no sooner…than”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The report consists ____ five sections.
fill-blanks.e: The phrase is “consists of”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: We must comply ____ the safety rules.
fill-blanks.e: The correct phrase is “comply with”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: He was indifferent ____ the criticism.
fill-blanks.e: The adjective takes “to”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The plan depends ____ the available budget.
fill-blanks.e: The phrase is “depends on”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: She takes pride ____ her work.
fill-blanks.e: The correct phrase is “take pride in”.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: He is senior ____ me by three years.
fill-blanks.e: Latin comparatives such as senior, junior and superior take 'to'.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: She has lived in Mumbai ____ 2015.
fill-blanks.e: 'Since' marks the starting point of a period continuing to now.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The book is divided ____ ten chapters.
fill-blanks.e: 'Divide into' shows the parts something is split into.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: I wish I ____ the answer yesterday.
fill-blanks.e: A wish about the past takes the past perfect.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: He is not used ____ getting up early.
fill-blanks.e: 'Be used to' + gerund means be accustomed to.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: She objected ____ his rude remarks.
fill-blanks.e: The verb 'object' takes 'to'.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: It is high time the government ____ steps to control pollution.
fill-blanks.e: 'It is high time' is followed by the past tense.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: Scarcely had the play begun ____ the lights went out.
fill-blanks.e: 'Scarcely … when' is the correct pairing.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: Not only the students but also their teacher ____ invited.
fill-blanks.e: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'teacher'.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: He prevented me ____ making a mistake.
fill-blanks.e: 'Prevent someone from doing something' is the fixed pattern.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The doctor, along with the nurses, ____ attending to the patient.
fill-blanks.e: 'Along with' does not change the subject; 'the doctor' is singular.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: Hardly ____ the meeting started when the power failed.
fill-blanks.e: 'Hardly' at the start takes past-perfect inversion: Hardly had the meeting started.

fill-blanks.p: Fill in the blank: The poor ____ always with us.
fill-blanks.e: 'The poor' (the + adjective) refers to people in general and is plural.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'break the ice' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: It means to ease tension at the start of a social situation.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'a piece of cake' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Used for tasks that need little effort.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'once in a blue moon' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: A blue moon is rare.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'hit the nail on the head' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To describe the problem or answer precisely.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'spill the beans' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To disclose confidential information.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'bite the bullet' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To endure a painful situation with courage.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'under the weather' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Slightly ill.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'cost an arm and a leg' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Extremely costly.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'burn the midnight oil' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To study or work long after dark.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'let the cat out of the bag' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To disclose something that was meant to stay hidden.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'the ball is in your court' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: It is your turn to act or decide
idioms-phrases.e: The next move is yours.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'cry over spilt milk' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Regret something that cannot be changed
w: Be very sad about a loss
idioms-phrases.e: Usually used in 'Don't cry over spilt milk'.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'beat around the bush' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Avoid coming to the main point
idioms-phrases.e: To talk about everything except the real issue.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'kill two birds with one stone' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Achieve two things with one action
idioms-phrases.e: A single effort solves two problems.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'once bitten, twice shy' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: A bad experience makes someone more cautious
w: A person repeats the same mistake gladly
idioms-phrases.e: A negative experience can make a person wary of similar situations.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'in hot water' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: The idiom describes being in difficulty or trouble.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'on the fence' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: A person on the fence has not chosen a side or made a decision.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'through thick and thin' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: It means remaining loyal or present through changing circumstances.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'a blessing in disguise' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Something that seems bad at first but leads to a good outcome
idioms-phrases.e: The eventual result reveals an unexpected benefit.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'back to square one' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Return to the beginning after a setback
idioms-phrases.e: A failed attempt forces someone to start over.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'take with a grain of salt' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: It advises not accepting a claim as entirely true without question.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'cut corners' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To skip steps to save time or money, usually at the cost of quality.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'on cloud nine' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Describes a state of great joy.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'call it a day' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To decide to stop an activity, usually work, for the time being.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'pull someone's leg' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To joke with someone by telling them something untrue.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'see eye to eye' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Usually used in the negative: 'They don't see eye to eye.'

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'miss the boat' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To be too slow to take advantage of a chance.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'get cold feet' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To lose courage just before doing something planned.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'throw in the towel' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: From boxing, where throwing in the towel concedes defeat.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'barking up the wrong tree' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Pursuing a mistaken idea or the wrong person
idioms-phrases.e: To look for a solution or culprit in the wrong place.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'add fuel to the fire' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To say or do something that intensifies a conflict.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'make ends meet' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To earn just enough to pay for basic needs.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'the tip of the iceberg' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: A small visible part of a much bigger problem
idioms-phrases.e: Most of an iceberg lies hidden below the water.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'keep one's fingers crossed' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Used when wishing for luck.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'turn a blind eye' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To pretend not to notice wrongdoing.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'a white elephant' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: A costly possession that is more trouble than it is worth
idioms-phrases.e: Something expensive to maintain and of little use.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'at the eleventh hour' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Just before it is too late.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'burn one's bridges' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Destroy any chance of going back
idioms-phrases.e: To act in a way that makes returning to a previous situation impossible.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'hold one's horses' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: Used to tell someone not to rush.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'bury the hatchet' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To end a conflict and become friendly again.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'steal someone's thunder' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Take attention or credit meant for someone else
idioms-phrases.e: To spoil someone's moment by doing their idea first.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'a red herring' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: A false lead that draws attention from the real issue.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'play second fiddle' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To be subordinate to someone else.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'take the bull by the horns' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: To deal with a problem directly and with courage.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'let sleeping dogs lie' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Avoid stirring up an old problem
idioms-phrases.e: Leave a settled matter alone to avoid trouble.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'cry wolf' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: From the fable of the shepherd boy whose false alarms were later ignored.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'hit the sack' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: An informal way of saying go to sleep.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'have a chip on one's shoulder' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Hold a grudge or feel resentful
idioms-phrases.e: To feel bitter about a past slight or unfairness.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'walk on eggshells' mean?
idioms-phrases.c: Be very careful not to upset someone
idioms-phrases.e: To act cautiously around a sensitive person or topic.

idioms-phrases.p: What does 'rule of thumb' mean?
idioms-phrases.e: A method based on experience rather than exact calculation.
